Recipe · software · Context & Guardrails · the read that earns the approval

Two-pass plan review

The clever way to hold it: a plan is flat to either eye alone — the depth you're approving lives in the disparity between two reads, never inside one.

Before you approve an agent's plan for a multi-file change, read it the way two eyes build depth — with two reads that catch different things: your situated read for the soft item only you can feel, and a second agent's branch-walk for everything you'd never hold in working memory. Neither read alone is the approval. The depth is computed from the gap.

The plan didn't gain depth because you stared harder with one eye. It was read twice, two different ways, and the gap fused.

Close one eye and the agent's plan is a flat page: three files, seven steps, a verification list, and an approve button already lit. Open the second eye and nothing on the page changes — yet now there's depth, and the depth is the only thing you were ever approving. It doesn't live in either read. It lives in the gap between them.

Left eye · your read

Shallow but situated.

You don't hold the whole design tree in working memory. What you hold is the nose: the soft item, the assumption that's wrong for this repo, the file that shouldn't be touched at all. You've seen what happens when the auth helper gets edited for a feature that had nothing to do with auth; the agent has never shipped your code on a Friday afternoon. That's the read no breadth can fake — and it's worthless until you make it specific.

So don't nod. In plan mode, pick keep planning with feedback, find one step, and quote its number and one word from it — because a quote forces the agent to revise the actual step, not nod at a vague worry:

not “looks good, one concern” — but “step 3, ‘update the auth helper’ — that's the wrong file for this change.”

↻ THEN CHECK THE REGENERATED STEP ACTUALLY SHARPENED.
“GOOD POINT” IS NOT A FIX. IF IT RE-SOFTENED, PUSH AGAIN — SAME QUOTE.

Right eye · agent walk-down

Exhaustive but unsituated.

The walk-down is your nose's inverse. Ask a second agent to dredge up every branch the plan left unresolved — the nullable-id question, the cache-or-live question, the retry-path question — including the dozen you'd never have kept in working memory. What it lacks is the nose: it can't feel which default would quietly break your codebase.

So run it as a sequence, not a dump. A list returns every branch at once; a read resolves them one at a time. Ask it to walk the branches it didn't resolve, one question with a recommended answer at a time, and let it run until it is out of branches:

you don't get to call it done early — and the recommendations are defaults, not prescriptions.

↻ REJECT AT LEAST ONE RECOMMENDATION THAT'S WRONG FOR THIS REPO.
IF YOU REJECTED NONE, YOU RUBBER-STAMPED THE SECOND READ TOO.

Fuse the two · the Monday-move is one line

Next multi-file plan an agent hands you, don't approve it — read it with the left eye and the right eye, approve only after both land, and the branch your push-back caught gets saved as a rule so the next plan in this repo arrives pre-shaped and the reading gets cheaper.

The proof you used both eyes, not one twice: you can name one thing your eye caught that the agent's walk-down never would have. If you can't, you read with one eye and called it depth — the agent did both passes and your situated read added nothing.

Where it sits: this is the personal foundation of Context & Guardrails. The same branch a second read surfaces is what a team later hardens into a shared judge or CI check — so the company's plan-quality stops depending on whether each person happened to read twice. (Positioning, not a coined law.)

The access surface

The principle: Map what you're protecting before you name what could go wrong.

A fire marshal counts every door out of a building before anyone games the break-in — so send a fresh subagent to walk the feature and chart every way in, while you keep your attention for the two doors only you can name: the one it drew too thin, and the one it never drew. Breadth is borrowed; judgment is yours.

Every door charted by the subagent. The two amber ones are yours — and STRIDE waits outside until the plan is whole.
The move that fails "Ship it, bolt the auth on later." Run the whole thing through STRIDE, then patch wherever it flinches. Both threat-model a vibe — six categories floating over a surface nobody actually charted.

Map a feature's access surface and you find most of the labour isn't yours. The entry points, the trust boundaries, the data tiers, the auth checkpoints — that's a long, structured breadth read, and a breadth read is exactly what you hand to a fresh subagent. Invoke a curated access-control skill, name the feature by route or a couple of symbols, and let it find the code itself — it burns its whole context window walking the tree, so yours stays clean for the part it can't do. What stays with you is two doors only you can name: the one it drew too thin, under-weighted against what you know this codebase actually does, and the one it never drew at all — the entrance that lives in your head and nowhere in the obvious code.

Make the read cover six surfaces, not five: entry points · trust boundaries crossed · data and its sensitivity tier · auth checkpoints, split into present, assumed, and delegated · external connector calls · and the load-bearing one — anything that bypasses, defers, or inherits an auth decision made elsewhere. That last door is where the surprises live. A generic reader handles standard middleware well and hand-rolled, inherited-elsewhere auth worst of all — which is precisely where breaches breed. A good skill doesn't fake omniscience; it narrates what it misses while it works — flags that a parent router's middleware propagates downward, flags bespoke auth it reads worse than the standard kind — then closes with a calibrated self-grade and names where the last percents hide. A flagged uncertainty beats a confident fabrication; those flags aren't noise to skim, they're invitations addressed to you.

The skill reads the standard doors well and the weird ones badly. The weird ones are where the break-ins happen.

The governing readSame feature, two readers. Breadth from the skill, depth from you — they converge on the delta note, and that join is the only thing STRIDE gets to read.

Now the door you can't delegate. Read the map's confessed blind spots — don't skim them — and write the delta: two surfaces, each reasoned in this codebase's own terms. One the skill flagged harder than you would have. One you know matters that it missed. Push every reason until it names something a different codebase wouldn't share. "This export route trusts the tenant id in the path, not the session" beats "check the auth." The first is yours; the second is anyone's. And the delta — not the skill's wall of output — is what STRIDE reads next. The raw map is the input to your judgment; the delta is the artifact. Each feature you map this way widens the kit the next feature's read starts from: the surface you name once, hardened into a team ADR, becomes default breadth the skill carries on its own — so the discipline compounds across features rather than resetting each time.

This week, the feature you're closest to shipping. Name it in one sentence, ask Claude Code to run the access-control skill on it as a subagent — no file paths — then write two lines: one door it flagged harder than you would have, one it missed that you know matters. The skill reads the tree; you write the delta, before your next PR review. You know it worked when both lines are present and neither is generic — and when the skill caught at least one thing you'd have missed.

Where it sits

This is the first guardrail in the trust arc: paired with STRIDE and the ADR under pressure, it walks a single engineer into staff-engineer and CISO review with a defensible map, a hardening decision, and a named residual risk. And that same chart-the-doors-before-the-build discipline is what scope-for-trust raises to company scope — the precondition for an org trusting an agent it didn't personally calibrate. Map a feature's access surface here; scope an agent's surface to what the org can trust there — same move, two surfaces.

Threat modeling before you build

The principle: threat modelling is only useful if it ends in a decision — STRIDE is the surface to reject most things against, not an oracle you beg for the attacks you missed.

Run STRIDE like a field guide's identification key — not telling you what the threat is, but what it isn't, one fork at a time, until one name is left. In real terms: point a subagent at the feature you're shipping, take the access surface it returns, walk the six STRIDE categories against that map, reject most with a one-word reason, name the single worst realistic incident — then write the survivor down as an ADR your whole team inherits instead of re-argues.

From a subagent's surface map to one ADR. The rejected forks are the deliverable — not off-cuts.
The move, in one line

Read STRIDE the wrong way round and it's a finder — an oracle you point at code, hoping it surfaces the attacks you missed. Read it the right way round and it's a surface you reject against: you fire all six categories expecting to throw most of them out, until the one threat that survives is left holding the page with its alternatives already weighed. But STRIDE has nothing to chew on without a surface map. So the move starts one rung earlier than the threat list — it starts with what you feed the model.

Don't aim the six categories at the code in your head; that's pub-quiz threat-modelling, free-associated attacks with nothing to reject against. Instead, run the access-control read as a subagent — point vanilla Claude Code at this week's feature and let it return who-reaches-what, through which checkpoint, under which trust boundary. That returned map is the specimen. The descent below runs against one real one: a billing webhook that re-hits the queue on retry. Walk STRIDE against that, and every rejection means something, because each is a door on the map you looked at and chose to leave shut.

Six STRIDE categories · walked against the map · reject most, on the record
1
S Spoofing — a forged sender impersonates the billing provider, signature faked. Reachable on this surface? reject · already signed
→ Signature is verified at the edge already → log it in Alternatives, read on. → next
2
T Tampering — the payload is altered in transit between provider and handler. Reachable? reject · mitigated · TLS
→ Transport is encrypted end-to-end → log it, read on. → next
3
R Repudiation — receipt of a webhook can't be proven later; no audit row written. Worth hardening? reject · acceptable risk
→ A missing audit row is a known, accepted cost here → log it, read on. → next
4
I Information-disclosure — a verbose error response leaks internal IDs to the caller. In scope? reject · out of scope
→ This surface returns no error body to the provider → log it, read on. → next
5
D Denial-of-service / retry-replay — the queue is at-least-once, so a retry storm replays the billing event and double-charges the customer. keep · the one
? A bounded, idempotent handler would make this benign — but it isn't bounded yet. Benign? no · live branch
descends to the leaf — the only fork that matches the worst-case story below
6
E Elevation-of-privilege — the queue worker draining the webhook runs as admin. In scope? reject · out of scope
→ Worker privilege is governed by a separate platform control → log it. Six categories exhausted. → resolved

When two forks both say keep, the worst realistic incident breaks the tie — not the most exotic attack, the one that would actually wake someone at 3am. A retry storm that double-charges a customer is that one, so couplet 5 holds the page. If your kept fork doesn't match the worst-case story, you optimised for the cheapest fix, not the real risk. Re-run it.

The survivor isn't a finding — it's a decision you write down. Four sentences in docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md, or whatever convention your repo already uses for decisions. Context — the worst realistic case. Decision — make the handler idempotent on event-id at the edge. Alternatives considered — every reject above, transcribed with its one-word reason, because the rejected forks are the argument that the survivor beat them. Constraint — the queue is at-least-once, so dedupe at the edge rather than trust the queue to promise exactly-once. The rest of the STRIDE output stays alongside as evidence, not as a hardening backlog you've quietly committed yourself to.

Notice what the ADR is not. It sits on disk, discoverable and named — but unlike a CLAUDE.md rules file, it does not auto-load into every future session. It's read when someone explicitly reaches for it, which is exactly the right weight for a decision: heavy enough to inherit, light enough not to nag the context window of every unrelated run. That distinction is the whole craft here — guardrails that fire every time go in the rules file; decisions that someone consults on purpose go in the ADR folder.

A threat held up against the five it beat is an argument. A threat picked from thin air is a vibe.

One honesty clause rides in the leaf. STRIDE is a tool, not the law. Coined by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg in a 1999 Microsoft threat-modelling memo and later sharpened by Adam Shostack in Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (2014), it's a mnemonic for six attack shapes — not a guarantee you caught yours. If the real risk is abuse-case or insider-threat shaped, STRIDE had no category for it: say so in Alternatives considered and reason in the lens that actually fit. The model gives you breadth fast; the codebase-specific judgement is yours to add, and it travels with the decision wherever it goes.

The compounding loop · the closing turn

Each ADR is the precedent the next threat-model starts from.

Here's why one defensible call outlives its single feature. Every engineer shipping an external surface carries one quiet unease — "I'm a bit nervous about that webhook." The trap isn't ignorance; you know roughly where the risk lives. The trap is that nobody made it a written decision, so the worry stays a private nerve: the staff engineer finds it in review, or prod finds it, and the team re-argues it from scratch on the next feature that touches the same surface. The write is the mechanism — a decision made under named pressure converts a private worry into shared, inheritable context. Map the surface, run STRIDE, reject most, write the ADR; then the loop closes onto the next feature, and the team's ADR folder is visibly thicker each pass.

One hardening decision is enough per feature; the team's breadth grows across many. The fourth time someone threat-models a surface like this billing webhook, they don't start from zero — they descend from the precedent the last engineer left. That's the difference between a security review that re-discovers the same threats every quarter and one that inherits them: the folder thickens, the re-arguing stops, and your CISO reads decisions instead of a backlog of TODOs.

How you know the threat was named · the test rides inline

A listed threat is not a named one.

The trap at the finish line is mistaking a long STRIDE list for a decision, so the test is falsifiable and runs on the ADR itself. First: the Context — or the scrollback — shows the worst-case story preceded the threat pick. Worst case first, then the choice; reversed order is menu-shopping and reads as reversed. Second: Alternatives considered names at least two rejected threats with a real reason each — acceptable risk, already mitigated, out of scope — not left dangling as backlog. Third, the sharpest tell: if the ADR could have been written without ever running the surface map, STRIDE was performative. The map's codebase-specific surfaces should be visible in the reasoning. A decision that reads like it came from a generic checklist probably did.

Monday move: pick one feature you're shipping this week with an external surface — a webhook, a public read, an action the agent now takes for a user. Vanilla Claude Code · access-control read as a subagent → STRIDE on what it surfaces · descend the six categories, rejecting most with a one-word reason · name the single worst realistic incident; the kept fork should match it · write the leaf in four sentences where your repo keeps decisions. The other threats stay alongside as evidence, not homework — and you arrive at review with the call already made.

Recipe · software lane · the move after a hardening call

The decision record

The contrarian read: the decision was the cheap part — what evaporates, and what you can't recover later, is the bearing that made it obvious.

A captain logs the bearing at the moment of the turn, because the sea will not hold the memory and a course reconstructed from a faint heading runs aground. Do the same with an architectural call made under pressure: while the why is still warm, write the four lines — context, decision, alternatives, and the one constraint that picked the winner — into a repo-resident file the next session reads cold. layer: personal→team→company · phase: Context & Guardrails

The contrarian read · what's actually expensive

You banked the decision. You lost the loaded context that made it obvious.

A threat-model pass flags one thing worth hardening. You weigh the trade-off, pick a side, ship the fix, and move on with the small relief of being past it. That relief is the trap. The intuition says the choosing was the hard part — but choosing is cheap. The expensive thing was loading the context that made one option obviously right: the attacker you were picturing, the alternative you rejected and why, the single constraint that broke the tie. That context decays fast and silently, and a feeling of having decided is not an artefact. A week later someone in review asks "why this and not the obvious alternative?" and you reconstruct a rationale you no longer actually hold — or defend a guess.

In an agentic workflow the decay costs twice. The agent that picks up adjacent work next week has no memory of the room where you decided. It reads the repo cold, sees a settled trade-off with no recorded reason, and does the rational thing — re-litigates the call from scratch, sometimes landing back on the option you already rejected, for the exact reason you already rejected it. The figure below is the whole pattern: one decision, two courses, split only by whether the bearing got logged while it was warm.

Same input, two outputs — because the bearing was logged, not lost. The fork is one four-line file.
The load-bearing line · what ages well

The verdict is in the diff. The constraint is the only thing that expires.

Here's the part the intuition gets backwards. The expensive thing to preserve isn't what you decided — anyone can read the diff and see you chose option X. The expensive thing is the constraint that made X obvious at the time. That single line is the test by which a future reader knows whether your call still holds when the inputs change. "We scoped the token to read-only because the endpoint is reachable unauthenticated" ages gracefully — the day the endpoint goes behind auth, anyone can see the call is now reversible. Strip the constraint and all that survives is a verdict with no expiry date, defended forever by reflex because nobody remembers what would falsify it.

A decision you can't reconstruct isn't a decision you still own — it's a guess you'll re-make under worse conditions.

The move, then, is not "document more." It's a shelf-life upgrade on a single decision: take the rationale that currently lives as a fading thought and turn it into a numbered file the repo carries forward. The convention most teams reach for is an Architecture Decision Record — a short, standalone, repo-resident note, one per decision, numbered so they read as a history. Not a wiki page that rots in a corner, not a Slack thread that scrolls away, not a commit message buried in history. A file the next session — yours or an agent's — cold-reads as part of the system's standing context. Four lines do the work:

the logbook entry — four lines, one decision
  1. Context. the threat you were picturing — e.g. an unauth read endpoint a STRIDE pass surfaced.
  2. Decision. the call you actually shipped — scope the token to read-only.
  3. Alternatives. what you weighed and dropped — gateway allow-list, per-call auth.
  4. The constraint that picked the winner. reachable unauthenticated — so least-privilege. This is the bearing. It's the one line that ages.

Default shape, not a mandate. The path docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md and the four sections are an illustrative default — if your repo already has an ADR convention, use theirs. The portable part is the discipline, not the directory name.

What thickens · the org stops storing reasoning in heads

One record is a note. A directory of them is the layer the next call rests on.

One ADR is a note. A repo of them is a different thing entirely — the layer the next decision rests on instead of fighting against. Each pass thickens the docs/adr/ directory, and each new constraint is read as standing context by whatever reads the repo next: a reviewer, a junior who wasn't in the room, a memory pass that loads prior decisions, or an agent doing adjacent work. Decision-recall stops depending on the person who made the call still being available — or still remembering. That's the systemic win: an org's architectural reasoning starts living in the codebase, not in senior heads. The one trap to refuse — treat the ADR as a checkbox after a menu-pick threat and you get paperwork: a fabricated trade-off written to satisfy a form. A genuine trade-off written down is design; a fabricated one is theatre. Write only what you actually decided.

So the move this week is small and immediate: after your next real trade-off, stop for ninety seconds while the why is still warm and log four lines into docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md (or wherever your repo keeps them) — context, the call, the alternative you rejected, and the constraint that decided it. You're not proposing a process or asking anyone's permission; an ADR is a markdown file in a directory you already own, and you're writing down a decision you already made. Do it once and the why stops evaporating; do it after every real call and the directory becomes the substrate every future reader — human or agent — inherits instead of reconstructs.

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software · Context & Guardrails · the first long send-off

Pre-sendoff gap-audit

The principle: the system you have is what gets tested — not the one you meant to build.

A field scientist leaves rows of the plot untreated on purpose — those bare strips are the only thing that can tell her what the treatment actually did. Same move, on context: before you send an agent off on a long run, have a subagent rank your CLAUDE.md, memory, ADRs and skills against the one real task, fill the worst three gaps, and leave the rest open on purpose — so the run reads them for you instead of your imagination.

You didn't patch the context clean. You ran a trial — filled the worst three, staked two open on purpose, pinned the SHA, let the run find the rest.
A context you filled everywhere tells you nothing

That bare-row trick is the whole pattern; the rest is plain agent mechanics. You already have a context system — a CLAUDE.md, a CLAUDE.local.md, a folder of observations, an ADR or two, a skill you authored last week. Each was written in its own moment, to fix the thing in front of you that day, and none of it was ever measured against the task you're about to send off. Read cold, the pile looks ready. That readiness is the illusion: a gap in context is invisible until a specific run leans on it. The first long send-off — multi-hour, sustained, the agent working without you watching — is the load that finally walks across the whole window at once and shows which lines are load-bearing for this task and which slots are simply empty.

Here's the part worth sitting with: over-preparing and pasting-and-hoping fail the same way. Close every gap the audit names and the run returns clean and tells you nothing — there was no open slot left to read the result against. Send the window as-is and you can't separate a real context failure from your own neglect: every slot is empty, so no single one is diagnostic. Both erased the control. The empty slot you leave on purpose, named in writing, is the one thing that turns the run from a delivery into a measurement.

The gap you leave open isn't a defect to close. Staked on purpose, it's the only instrument you've got.

The gap-audit · patch vs. trialFill every gap and the run is fine and silent. Stake two slots open and the agent breaks where you can read it. Three fills is a deliberate teaching budget — not a measured optimum.
Scope one task, stake two gaps, send it off

Run it Monday. Pick one task off your backlog you've meant to hand an agent — multi-hour, real, a 'done' you can say in a sentence. Not an epic, not a typo-fix. It has to be specific enough that a single run will exercise the whole context window at once. Then point a subagent at your CLAUDE.md · CLAUDE.local.md · observations · ADRs · skills and have it rank where the context runs thin against that task. It returns a ranked gap list — and the trap is reverence. Push back: the ranking is a hypothesis about your holes, not a verdict you clear. It over-weights the tidy gaps it can name and misses the assumption baked so deep nobody wrote it down. You're the one who knows which one this task will actually hit.

Fill the worst three — and watch for the one trap sharp enough to name. A gap will look like "a real code change, I'll skip it", and if you skip it the run fails in a boring way: wrong DB assumption, stale config, something you'd have caught in ten seconds. If the audit calls it context, it's context, even when the fill is one rule ("we use Postgres, not Mongo"). The whole point of the run is the interesting break — the one only your next move can diagnose. Then the two gaps you're leaving: stake each one in writing, with why. Those notes are the instrument.

Now pin the starting point — commit current state on a feature branch, note the SHA and the transcript path — and dispatch the scoped task in the same session, un-packaged: no plan.md, no verifier. Let it run with your rules, memory, ADRs and skills loaded as they stand, and walk away. When the trace comes back, read it against the slots you staked open: next time you fill the gaps a real run surfaced, not the ones you imagined at the desk, and your context carries a richer, evidence-fed load into every send-off after.

The two staked gaps · read these as labelled, not literal

“Three” is a deliberate teaching budget for a first un-packaged run, not a measured optimum. Under-fill on purpose so the run can teach you; there's no law that filling three gaps maximises learning.

“Un-packaged” is a sequencing choice, not a claim that un-packaged runs are better. It's a first step to expose failure modes — packaging is the right move once you've seen what un-packaged gets wrong.

The three-block memory frame the audit leans on travels as a frame for naming what you've already built, not a template to fill in. It makes an empty slot legible; it is not a checklist to author against.

This is the personal-layer habit that keeps a context system honest at scale. One person who audits and deliberately under-fills produces evidence-fed gaps instead of imagined ones — and that same discipline, test against a real run and fill from what it exposed, is what keeps a team's shared kit and a company's memory layer growing from real failures rather than from policy no one's work ever validated.

The Work
The Work
Recipe · business lane · phase: The Work · the more-than-one-mind move

Splitting work across agents

You keep hiring three of the same agent — then act surprised the committee agrees with itself.

Adding a second agent is a hire, and the screening question is the one any honest hiring manager asks: does it reach somewhere the first can't, read a source the first doesn't, or hold a position the first won't? If not, you have one prompt in three costumes. When the difference is real, the move is to make the agents disagree on disk and force a framework to pick — not let a chat smooth the friction away. SCOPE · personal → team → company: a single builder's split becomes the org's standing way of staffing a question.

One prompt in three blazers — or three agents, three context files, one judge. The filesystem is the meeting room.

You almost ran it: staff this question with three agents, because three minds beat one and the org chart looks serious. Here is what the impressive shape won't tell you. You keep filling three seats with the same agent — same sources read, same dialect spoken, same opinion held — and then you're surprised the committee agrees with itself. A second agent that reaches what the first reaches, talks how the first talks, and leans the way the first leans is not a colleague. It's a prompt you photocopied twice and paid to run three times. So before you split anything, run the interview.

Round oneThe screen — name the forcing axis or close the req

Three agents, or one prompt in three costumes?

Hold the three candidates side by side and ask the only screening question that matters: does any of them reach a source the others can't, read it in a language the others don't, or argue a position the others won't? Three agents pointed at the same context window, retrieving the same documents, reasoning in the same register and landing the same conclusion are not three agents. They are one prompt that owns three costumes — and they will outvote your doubts three-to-nothing, because they were never built to disagree.

So name the difference out loud, on exactly one axis. Access: they literally reach different things — one is scoped to the internal wiki, one to the data warehouse, one to the open web. Dialect: the sources don't speak the same language and shouldn't be flattened into one before you've read them apart. Stance: the question needs a planner, a skeptic, and a reframer arguing, not one agent averaging the three in a single pass. If you can't put your finger on which axis is making one agent impossible, you don't have a panel — you have one prompt cosplaying as three, and the coordination cost is pure waste.

Can't name the axis? Close the req. You just kept the coordination cost in your pocket and lost nothing.

Round twoDon't let them rehearse the same answer — separate sessions, separate files

Give each agent its own source zone and forbid the green room.

Once the difference is real, the worst move is to run all three in one thread and let them reconcile as they go. Sizing a market is the canonical case, because the answer is genuinely three answers in three dialects: the loud answer — press releases, analyst forecasts, the figures everyone repeats; the academic answer — benchmarks, papers, the careful caveated version; and the quiet answer — practitioner blogs, repo activity, what people say once the slides are off. Give each its own session scoped to one source zone, and forbid them to compare notes before they write.

Where they write is the point: not a chat, but the disk. The filesystem is the meeting room. One file per source zone — loud.md · academic.md · quiet.md — non-comparable on purpose. A chat thread is built to reconcile; it quietly resolves the conflict on the way through, and the disagreement you split to find dies there. A file just records what its agent saw, and lets the contradiction sit on disk long enough for a judge to read it. Nothing needs procuring first: several sessions on one working directory already run, so you open two more in the folder you're already in.

Three files, three dialects, no green room. The seam you'd have lost in conversation is now sitting on disk.

Round threeThe panel, not one tired interviewer — distinct stances under a rubric

A judge that argues beats one agent averaging three files.

Synthesis is not one tired agent reading three files and quietly splitting the difference. Point a judge at the three files and give it distinct stances to hold — a planner, a what-would-have-to-be-true skeptic, and a reframer (that trio is the default starting line-up, not the only correct one — swap a seat if your question fits a different argument). Then bind the judge to a rubric that forces one question before it writes a sentence of synthesis: where do these three contradict each other?

Drop the rubric and the judge does what any model does at a fork — it rounds the corner and makes peace. Hand three conflicting files to an un-briefed synthesiser and you get a fluent, reasonable, utterly beige consensus, the very thing you opened three sessions to avoid. The rubric is the judge's spine: "show me where these disagree, before you write a word." Without it you have built an expensive route back to the single-agent answer.

A briefed judge picks a direction; an un-briefed one hedges. The rubric is what makes it choose.

Round fourThe reference you keep — and the one you can run on Monday

Write down which seat earned its desk, then start there.

After the answer lands, don't bin the interview notes. In the review, write down which session actually earned its keep and which was the photocopy you should have screened out — into the root ./CLAUDE.md that governs how the next question gets staffed: this zone was noise, that stance was redundant, the rubric needed a sharper "show me the seam." That one sharpening clause is the whole compounding mechanism — the first time you split a question you're guessing at the division of work; by the third you're not, because the next split starts from earned rules a teammate inheriting the folder reads from too.

So here is Monday, and it's smaller than the diagram. Take one question you keep getting beige back on from a single agent. Write down which one of access, dialect, or stance is forcing the split — if you genuinely can't name one, stop, keep the single agent, and pocket the coordination cost. If you can name it, open two sessions on the same folder, point each at a different source zone, and make each write its own file before anything synthesises. Two sessions · two files · no third agent yet · no rubric yet. Then read the two files side by side and notice the seam you would have lost in a single chat.

By the third question you're not guessing at the org chart — you're staffing it against rules that earned their lines.

The exit test

You passed only if a colleague reading the synthesis can see where the three disagreed — and the answer is specific enough to act on with its gaps left plainly visible.

That's a harsher bar than "looks thorough." The seam has to show, because the judge picked a direction instead of hedging the three into a mush. And then the test most candidates-for-splitting fail, which is the entire point: if one good prompt would have produced the same answer, you didn't run a panel — you paid three salaries for one opinion. Most questions live on that side of the line. The discipline is learning the move and respecting the default.

Close the req. Keep the single agent. That is a pass too.

The Work
Recipe · business lane · The Work

The validation gate

The principle: Hybrid beats autonomous — the move that scales is not "remove the human," it's "put the human in the one place that matters."

Think of the run like a canal lock: water rises and falls freely on either side, but there is one chamber where the level changes for good, and that is where the gate sits. Find the step in the agent run that can't be undone, gate exactly there — and let the run flow everywhere else.

Personally it's the discipline that lets you ship an agent without betting what you can't take back; at company scope it's the architecture that decides where autonomy is allowed to touch the irreversible — the org-level guardrail every customer-facing, money-moving, data-touching deployment composes against, and the move that turns "should we automate this?" from a vibe into a placed gate.

Drop the lock now — the rest is plain agent plumbing. A run has steps: it drafts, it classifies, it routes, it sends. Most of those steps are reversible — a bad draft gets re-drafted, a wrong classification gets re-routed, and nothing left the building. Then there's the one step where the level changes for good: the refund wired, the email sent, the record updated, the migration committed. The gate is not about how good the model is. It's about which step can't be undone. Same agent, same accuracy — a 5% error rate is fine on a step you can roll back and catastrophic on a step you can't.

Mark the run

List the steps; tag each reversible or not.

Most teams never do this — the demo blurred the steps into one autonomous blur. Writing them out is the whole analysis. Beside each step in the run, reversible or not, honest about which actions actually reach a customer, move money, or change a record you can't roll back. The first not is where the level changes for good.

Place the gate

Put a human exactly on the irreversibility line — and nowhere else.

Let the run generate at full speed up to that step. Then one human: approve, reject, modify. Not a reviewer reading everything — that's just slow autonomy. The gate is cheap: a named approver, a one-step sign-off in a chat thread, a named owner in a doc. The artefact is the placed gate, not the agent. Past it, the run executes; execution is mechanical once approved.

Watch the level

Keep a human monitoring — the line moves.

The irreversibility line isn't fixed forever. A step that needed approval when the agent was new might, after a thousand verified runs without incident, be reclassifiable as safe to automate — or a near-miss might reveal a step you'd mis-tagged as reversible. Every escalation is a flag on a step; every near-miss is data, not bad luck. The step map is a living document: review it when the workflow changes, when the model updates, when volume jumps an order of magnitude. That's how the line gets re-drawn on evidence rather than optimism — and the re-tagging is exactly the operational context a compounding system is built to keep, so the next placement is faster and more grounded than this one.

The honest part · where the line is still moving

The claim is real — and so is the edge it stops at.

I won't sell you "gates always win." The named reversals that make this vivid — Zillow's algorithmic home-buying programme ($500M write-down), Arup's fraudulent ~$25M wire, Air Canada's tribunal-enforced hallucinated fare policy — are illustrative examples drawn from a convergence finding (15+ independent signals across 10 domains, assembled March 2026; practitioner reports, vendor reversals, consumer studies, analyst predictions). They aren't proof on their own; the evidence is the convergence. And the counter-evidence travels with the claim: a minority of practitioners — around 22% in one survey — report full-replacement success in bounded, well-scoped domains, and some customer-service deployments match human satisfaction (WeightWatchers cited at 4.6/5, SeatGeek at comparable CSAT).

So here's what I can't yet tell you: where exactly your irreversibility line sits — and it won't sit still. The December 2025 coding shift moved it; the next model release will move it again.

That's not a hole in the move — it is the move. "Hybrid beats autonomous" holds at the high-stakes, high-volume, irreversible end; it is not a law of nature that gates always outperform. Refusing to fake the number is what keeps the gate placement honest, because the only way to find your line is to mark your own run and watch what the monitor surfaces. The deliverable isn't a fixed answer. It's a placed gate you keep re-checking.

Convergent evidence as of the March 2026 finding — not a controlled result. The 85%-per-step / ~20%-over-10-steps figure used elsewhere is an illustrative calculation of how errors compound down a chain, not a measured benchmark.

Monday

Take one workflow you've already pointed an agent at. Write its steps in a line — the literal run, step by step. Beside each, write reversible or not, honest about which actions actually reach a customer, move money, or change a record you can't roll back. Circle the first not. That circle is your lock — the one chamber where the level changes for good. Name who approves it and what would make them say no. One list, one circle, ten minutes — and you've turned "can we just let it run?" from a vibe into a step you can point at.

one list · one circle · ten minutes
The Work
Recipe · software lane · The Work

Packaging a run

The principle: the prompt was never the thing you write — the packaging is, and the short prompt only invokes it.

You think the work of sending off a long agent task is wording the prompt. It isn't. The wording barely matters; what the agent finds on disk decides everything. Move the effort there and you can step away.

The thing you were optimising · was the wrong thing

The prompt is the least of it.

Here is the move most people get backwards. They labour over the prompt — phrasing the objective just so, stacking caveats, hoping a perfect paragraph will survive a four-hour run. It won't. A long agent task has a physics problem: the context window fills from the bottom, recent tokens outweigh early ones, and by hour two the careful objective you typed is scroll archaeology. The agent navigates from recency, not intent. No paragraph, however well-built, anchors against that.

So stop writing the prompt and start building the run. The agent re-orients against files on disk, not against the sentence that launched it — so that is where the steering lives.

Three failure modes do most of the damage on long runs, and practitioners who've hit the wall name them consistently (Ronacher, Cherny, Klaassen — a convergent pattern, not an official Claude Code taxonomy): drift, where the goal shifts as recency overwrites intent; rot, where the agent cold-starts after a session restart and re-invents the plan from nothing; and plausible-but-wrong, where the output reads correct because nothing checked it against a stable definition of done — and a model trained to be helpful will frame a partial failure as a partial success. You cannot out-phrase these. You package against them.

What does the work instead · one file per failure mode
reference.md
closes drift

Half a page: the goal as a testable outcome, the constraints the agent must not violate, the definition of done. Task-local — it lives beside the run, not in your codebase rules. The agent re-reads it to confirm goal.

plan.md
closes rot

The state carrier. It reads clean on a cold start, so the agent picks up where it left off across a session restart and you never re-explain where it got to. Mid-run, when it drifts, it re-reads this instead of improvising.

verifier · stable path
closes plausible-but-wrong

A check at a fixed path — shell-hook, LLM-judge, or Ralph re-feed. Pick the shape against your dominant failure, not the safest one. It fires pass-or-fail on the output, so self-report stops being the only gate.

One thing makes the lesson legible: pin the SHA before you touch anything. Commit current state on a named branch, record the short SHA, and fork the packaged re-send from it. Now the un-packaged run and the packaged run start from the same codebase, and the diff between them reads as clean signal rather than confound. That contrast is the whole point. If the two runs come out the same, packaging wasn't doing work — which tells you the real failure is upstream (bad scope, wrong slice, missing context no kit can supply). More useful to know that than to ship a run nobody was really checking.

And it compounds, because the first reference.md is never quite right and the first verifier catches the obvious while missing the interesting. You only learn what the kit was missing by reading what fired. After each run, tighten reference.md against what drifted, recalibrate the verifier against what it missed, improve plan.md's format where the agent got confused — then re-send. The kit earns its shape from real failure, not prophylactic policy, and that verifier quietly becomes your first eval — the foundation the team-scale eval practice is later built on. This is the personal-reliability floor of the software lane: you can't promote a packaged send-off the team hasn't seen you run, and the whole kit is three markdown files, a short script, and two git commands — all of it in your terminal before you say a word to anyone.

Right now: open the last long-running task you sent off and ask it the plain question — does it have a plan.md? a reference.md? a verifier at a stable path? Pick the one that's missing, write the half-page version in the next fifteen minutes — goal, constraints, done criteria — pin the SHA, and send the same task again. Read the two runs side by side.

You were never paid to write a better prompt. You were paid to build a run that finishes the job while you're somewhere else — and the prompt is just the doorbell.

The Work
Recipe · the work · software mat · personal throughput

Run N tasks in parallel

The principle: one session per working directory — isolate the tree, reconcile on the shared graph.

Give each parallel task its own working directory on its own branch, all sharing one Git history — so three agents can run at once without clobbering each other's files. The personal unlock that becomes a team's collision-free contribution model.

Three trees, one root. The model was never the bottleneck — the single working tree was.
The mechanism · why a branch isn't enough

Same two branches — the question is whether the tree moves under the session.

Once you trust the agent on one thing, the obvious move is to run it on three: a bug here, a refactor there, a small feature in a third corner. The hour you spent on one task could carry three. Then you point a second session at the same folder and they start clobbering each other. The reflex fix — git checkout a different branch — is worse than useless here: it overwrites the working tree in place. The editor and the running session are suddenly staring at file contents that changed under them; the session's scrollback now references files that no longer look the way it remembers, and the next turn goes sideways.

A clone fixes the collision the heavy way — a full second copy on disk, history severed — which is overkill for "I want two branches at once." Worktrees are the middle path: one repo, many working directories, each checked out to its own branch, all sharing the same underlying Git history. Switching between them is cd, not git checkout. Your original directory stays exactly where it was — zero checkout churn. The diagram below puts the two tracks side by side: same two branches, the only difference is whether the tree moves under the session.

Process diagram · 01A branch switch moves the tree under the running session; a worktree gives each branch its own directory, so cd replaces checkout and nobody loses their footing.

That's the whole reason the field reaches past branches and clones. Each option buys isolation; only one buys it without giving something up you needed to keep. Branches are cheap but pay at switch time — the session's footing. Clones are isolated but heavy — disk, plus a severed history that no longer reconciles. Worktrees give isolation without divergence: N working trees, one shared commit graph, so the sessions can't collide on disk yet every change still rides the same history and reconciles at merge. The upgrade picture below tags each step with what it actually costs you.

The bottleneck on running more agents was never the model. It was that one repo gave you one working directory.

Process diagram · 02Branches cost the session's footing; clones cost disk and a shared graph. Worktrees give isolation and shared history at once — and enforce the invariant for free.

The named principle reads like a tooling tip and is actually the thing the whole pattern protects: one session per working directory. Every collision failure mode — clobbered edits, stale scrollback, sideways turns — traces back to violating it. Two sessions in one folder and the later write wins; the earlier session's in-progress edit is gone from disk while its scrollback still believes the old content. Worktrees aren't the goal. They're the cheapest way to make the invariant hold while still running N sessions, which is precisely why Boris Cherny calls parallel worktrees the single biggest productivity unlock — a named practitioner's stance (Jan 2026 X thread + Pragmatic Engineer interview), not a measured or benchmarked finding.

The discipline keeps going past the start. Don't make one session narrate to the other what it did — that's asking two conversations to stay in sync by hand. Let Git carry the bits: commit, push a branch, or git stash push / cd / git stash pop. And when two worktrees touch the same file, the conflict surfaces cleanly at merge — Git stops both and shows the markers. This is the one place the human stays in the driver seat. Agents are confident and don't always read carefully enough at a merge boundary; you know what each change was for, Git knows the lines, you put them together. Do not let either agent auto-resolve.

The honest part: refuse to parallelise when serial is faster. Three cases earn a serial run. Ordering dependencies — a migration, then a backfill, then the reader code — where step three against pre-step-one state buys nothing and risks corruption. Greedy parallelism on small tasks, where the worktree coordination plus the conflict recovery loses to just doing the two tasks in sequence. And the case where you're still learning what "good" looks like in one session — a second session adds variables, not learning. The win is wall-clock time saved, not worktrees created. The loop below shows where the human stays in it.

Process diagram · 03Send N → run isolated → ride the graph → resolve conflicts by hand → git worktree remove. Each pass the trunk absorbs more parallel work without the sessions ever colliding.
Test · how you know it worked

Three sessions run for an hour and none of them gets confused about what's on disk — each has its own scrollback, its own working directory, its own branch, and none references file contents that changed under it.

When two worktrees did touch the same file, the collision shows up as a clean merge conflict you resolve by hand — not as a silently overwritten edit you discover later. And the honest negative test: if you spent more time coordinating worktrees and recovering from conflicts than the tasks would have taken in sequence, the parallelism was the wrong call.

Use when

You trust the agent on one thing and now want it on three — a bug, a refactor, a small feature — but the moment you point a second session at the same folder, they clobber each other.

Build

Sibling worktree directories, each on its own branch, one session each, all sharing one Git history — removed with git worktree remove once merged.

Test

Collisions arrive as clean merge conflicts.
Not as silently clobbered edits.

Core moves

One repo, N working directories, zero collisions

Two git commands and the restraint to stop there.
1

Add a worktree per task

Not a branch. A sibling directory on its own branch — git worktree add -b.

2

One session per folder

The invariant. Never two in one directory — the later write wins.

3

Let Git carry the bits

Commit, push, or stash. Don't make one session narrate to the other.

4

Resolve at merge by hand

Read the diff. Pick which line wins — no agent auto-resolve.

5

Refuse when serial wins

Ordering deps · tiny tasks · still learning. Wall-clock is the test.

add worktree→one session each→Git carries the bits→merge by hand→remove

Then it scales: isolate the tree, reconcile on the shared graph, resolve by hand. The same discipline a whole team relies on when many contributors run many agents against one codebase.

Monday move: two unrelated tasks already in your backlog. A bug and a small refactor that don't depend on each other. git worktree add -b <task> ../<repo>-<task> · twice · one session in each. If they turn out to depend on each other, you learned the "when NOT to" lesson the cheap way. Worktrees ship with Git — the only thing you need permission for is your own restraint.

Why
The principle

One session per working directory. Isolate the tree; reconcile on the shared graph.

"One repo, many working directories — the model was never the bottleneck; the single working tree was."

Worktrees break the one-to-one between a repo and its working directory. The mechanism is isolation without divergence: N working trees, one shared history, so the sessions can't clobber each other on disk yet every change still rides the same commit graph and reconciles at merge. Branches gave cheap isolation but overwrote the tree under the running session; clones gave isolation but severed the history. Worktrees are the move that gives you both at once.

Which is why Boris Cherny calls parallel worktrees the single biggest productivity unlock — one named practitioner's stance (Jan 2026 X thread + Pragmatic Engineer interview), not a quantified or benchmarked result. Read the claim as a practitioner pointing at the lever, not as proof of a number. The lever itself is plain: the invariant the whole pattern protects is one session per working directory, and a worktree is the cheapest way to make it hold while still running N sessions.

Isolate the tree. Reconcile on the graph. Resolve by hand.
Verification
Verification
Recipe · R5 · verification · business lane

Earn a judge by benchmarking

The principle: Empirical method selection over authority — the scoreboard is the source of trust, not the method's pedigree.

Stop trusting quality checks and start measuring them — by running several detectors on the same claim pool and reading the scoreboard that names the winner.

The scoreboard is how you earn the authority the rubric claimed. The table is a mock — the figures are placeholders, the real ones come from your run.
The mechanism · why the rubric is the weakest possible authority

The rubric you trusted most is the one you measured least.

Here is the uncomfortable arithmetic of pre-written rubrics: you write the check list before you know what the agent will get wrong. The rubric is calibrated to your expectations, not to the agent's failure modes. It passes everything it was never designed to catch — and you will not discover this until a claim slips through and someone downstream notices. By which point the authority you thought you'd built is borrowed time.

The move that fixes this is empirical rather than authoritative. Pull the actual claims the agent produced. Adjudicate them yourself — grounded, overreach, or fabricated — against the sources you have. Now you are the ground truth. Run several candidate detectors against that same pool, each writing results to its own file, none blended. Read the scoreboard: one detector won on precision and coverage; another had better recall but missed half the overreach cases. The data names the winner. That is a judge you can defend.

The default in Agents 101 Module 5 starts with thirty claims — enough to prove the method on your own output. (Illustrative default — production judges scale to hundreds of claims and running corrections; the method is fixed, the benchmark size is not.) The size is not the point; adjudicating those claims yourself is. You cannot benchmark a judge you haven't run on real output you actually produced.

Process diagram · 01Four detectors, one claim pool, one adjudicator. The scorer reads all four against your verdicts and the row that won earned the judge file. No blending before scoring.
The crossing move · from opinion to infrastructure

The benchmark is what separates a decision from a guess.

There is a category error that survives most AI pilots: using a rubric as if it were a test. A rubric tells you what good looks like in advance; a benchmark tells you whether your detector finds good in practice. These feel similar from the outside — both involve a list and a tick — but their epistemic weight is completely different. The rubric's authority is the writer; the scoreboard's authority is the data. One of these survives a pointed question from a sceptical stakeholder; the other doesn't.

The crossing move is the benchmark itself — not a new tool, not a platform. You already have the output. You already have the sources. Twenty minutes adjudicating ten claims builds the ground truth half. From that moment you can run a candidate detector and score it. Nothing required that isn't in a plain text editor and the output you produced yesterday.

⚠ Two honest labels, stated once. The hero scoreboard is an illustrative mock — its precision and recall are placeholders for shape, not figures from a measured run; the only real numbers are the ones you produce on your own output. And "30 claims" is a pedagogically calibrated default from Agents 101 Module 5, not a validated production minimum — production judges scale to hundreds of claims and running corrections. The method is fixed; both the numbers and the pool size are yours to fill in.
Process diagram · 02The crossing move is the benchmark — the same output, the same sources, twenty minutes to adjudicate. On the left: opinion. On the right: scoreboard. One of these survives cross-examination.

There is a side effect worth naming. Running the benchmark teaches you what the agent actually gets wrong — claim by claim, not in aggregate. The overreach cases are more instructive than the fabrications; the fabrications are obvious, the overreach is where a defensible agent walks into indefensible territory without either party noticing. That knowledge is structural. It flows back into the guardrail file, the context you provide, the constraints you place on the next generation pass. The benchmark is not a one-time quality gate. It's a diagnostic that sharpens the upstream build.

The scoreboard also teaches you to evaluate evaluators — and that move transfers. You bench-tested groundedness today. Tomorrow it's tone. Next month it's brand compliance or regulatory language. The specific domain is incidental; the empirical method is permanent. Every future quality question you automate follows the same recipe. That is why this pattern sits at a gate, not a tip.

A judge you benchmarked beats a rubric you trusted in advance. The margin is the same as the pilot over the press release.
Process diagram · 03The judge you earned becomes the yardstick the work tightens against. Each eval pass surfaces misses; misses sharpen the next benchmark's claim pool; the known limit gets more precise. This is how a small benchmark grows into production infrastructure.
What "Test" actually means · the scoreboard read

A colleague reads the scoreboard and explains why this judge won.

The test for a benchmarked judge is not the precision number. The number can be right by chance. The test is whether a colleague — one who wasn't in the room when you ran it — can read the scoreboard and say: here is why detector 1 won, here is the claim shape detector 3 missed, here is what the known limit line covers. If they can, the authority has transferred. If they can't, the judge is not a judge; it's a number with a label.

The known limit line is not an admission of failure. It is the most important line in the file. Every detector has a reach boundary; the judge that names its boundary is the one that doesn't fail silently. A narrow judge that works beats a broad judge that pretends — because the broad judge fails on the exact claim shapes the team assumes it caught. Name the limit once, written down, and the team can reason around it.

Use when

Quality matters enough that "looks good" is not a decision method — and someone will eventually ask: how do you know the judge works? Recurs after any first agent build producing text with downstream consequences, at the moment a team considers trusting agent output for external audiences, whenever the output sits at uneasy distance from the sources.

Build

A 30-claim benchmark (illustrative default — scale in production): evidence roster + claim pool + adjudicated verdicts. A detector scoreboard. A judge file with the winning detector configured and a "Known limit:" line that names what it cannot reach.

Test

A colleague reads the scoreboard and explains why this judge won and where it stops — without asking you.
Not merely "it scored well."

Core moves

Five moves that earn the judge its row

Quality authority shifts from trust to evidence in five moves.
1

Pull claims from the real output

Not a hypothetical. The actual thing. Thirty claims is the default — illustrative; scale in production.

2

Adjudicate against sources yourself

Grounded / overreach / fabricated. You are the ground truth. This is what makes everything downstream defensible.

3

Run candidate detectors blind

Each writes to its own file. No blending before scoring. Four is a good starting count.

4

Score precision, recall, coverage

Read the scoreboard row by row. The data names the winner — not the method's reputation.

5

Package winner as a judge file

Configured detector plus a "Known limit:" line naming what it cannot catch. A narrow judge that works beats a broad one that pretends.

benchmark→earn judge→run eval loop→surface misses→sharpen benchmark

Then the judge is infrastructure, not a one-time check. Every eval pass makes the next benchmark's claim pool sharper. The specific domain changes; the empirical method stays.

Fastest entry point: any output you already have. Pull ten claims (not thirty — just ten). Open the sources. Adjudicate each one. Plain text file · agent prompts for detectors · markdown for the judge · ~20 min. You've built the ground truth half. Everything else follows.

Why
The principle

Empirical method selection over authority. The scoreboard is the source of trust, not the method's pedigree.

"A judge you benchmarked beats a rubric you trusted in advance."

The rubric you trust most in advance is the weakest possible quality authority — you calibrated it to your expectations before the agent ran, before you knew which claim shapes it would miss. The benchmark flips that entirely. You pull real claims from real output, adjudicate them yourself, and the data names the winner. You walk out with a judge you'd defend in a meeting, not a document you'd apologise for.

There is a subtler transfer: running the benchmark teaches you to evaluate evaluators — and that move applies to tone, brand, compliance, any quality dimension you'll ever automate. The domain is groundedness. The skill is empirical method selection. Every future quality question in the operating model follows the same recipe.

This is also the personal quality gate: the moment you stop trusting agent outputs and start measuring them. Without it, every downstream quality claim at team or company level rests on opinion. With it, the authority is owned, transferable, and defensible — which is what makes the next autonomy rung earnable rather than asserted.

The method you measured beats the method you read about by the same margin the pilot beats the press release.
Test in practice

Hand the scoreboard to a colleague who wasn't in the room. Ask them: why did detector 1 win? Where does it stop? If they can answer — from the file, not from memory — the judge is earned.

If they say "it scored highest" without explaining the claim shapes it missed and the ones it caught, the scoreboard isn't readable enough yet. That's the edit: make the recall gap visible in the table, not just in the number. A readable scoreboard is part of the artefact.

Verification
Recipe · R6 · business lane · phase: verification

The fixed-judge loop

The principle: a yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick — freeze the standard and let the work chase it.

Treat the standard like the platinum cylinder that was the kilogram — one object held still on purpose, never edited — then put the rest down and work in real agent terms. You write your quality bar into one judge.md, point a separate generator agent at it, and feed every correction the judge returns into a tactic file — never the judge. One file moves round after round; one never does. That's how a standard stops being one desk you sit at and becomes a file a whole team's agents can run against, unattended.

One agent loop, three rounds. tactic.md chases; judge.md holds.
The mechanism · which file is allowed to move

Pin the standard; let the work chase it.

Start with the inversion, because it's the whole pattern. In make output yours you steer a fresh agent by changing the input — you edit the prompt, the CLAUDE.md, the sources in context, until the output drifts to follow. Here you run it backwards: you pin the standard so the output can't hide behind a moving target, and let the generation chase it. The standard lives in one file — call it judge.md — and you declare it untouchable for the run. The generator's how-to lives in a second file, tactic.md, and that one is allowed to thicken. One file moves; one does not.

Lose that discipline and you measure nothing. The seductive failure feels like diligence: you set out to improve a recurring output, so each round you sharpen the work — and, while you're in there, you sharpen judge.md too. A tighter criterion here, a kinder threshold there. Round three scores higher than round one and you congratulate yourself. But the work and the yardstick both moved, so the number is hollow: you cannot tell whether the work got better or the bar got softer. A score is only comparable when the thing producing it stays fixed. Freeze the judge, and round three's number finally has something honest to say about round one.

Process diagram · 01The inverse of steering. Here the standard is pinned and the work moves toward it — a later round is comparable to an earlier one only because the judge held still.

One structural rule makes the whole thing honest: the agent that writes the work and the agent that grades it must be different. Run them as two separate sessions, with two separate prompts — the generator reads tactic.md and writes a draft; the grader reads judge.md and the draft, and returns flags. A single agent grading its own output drifts, slowly and plausibly, toward flattering itself — not from malice, but because inside one context the cheapest way to score higher is to soften what counts as good. The asymmetry is the design: one part writes and wants to pass, one part rejects and owes nothing. Nothing marks its own homework.

Freezing the judge looks like giving up control. It's the opposite: it's your taste, delegated and made durable.

The upgrade · from reading every draft to designing the loop

You stop reviewing outputs. You start designing the loop.

The reason this matters to you is brutally practical. Today the recurring check — the weekly board narrative, the customer release blurb, the renewal-risk read — runs because you run it. You are the bottleneck and the quality bar at once, and the day you're on a plane the bar travels with you. Lift your standard out of your head into judge.md, and a generator agent can chase it while you do something else entirely. The restraint to leave that one file alone is the entire price of admission — and it's the move from operator to owner.

One lap, logged

Not a recipe — a single run, in order. Pick one recurring output you currently sanity-check yourself — the weekly board note, the customer release blurb. Then watch which file is allowed to move.

00:00 · write
Write the standard that output must meet into a one-page judge.md — the criteria you'd apply by hand. Then make one promise: I do not touch this file again this run. Save it. From here it's the cylinder under glass.
00:04 · split
Open two separate agent sessions — one writes the draft against tactic.md, one grades it against the frozen judge.md. Nothing marks its own homework; the separation is the whole integrity of the lap.
00:10 · round one
Generate the draft. The grader returns its flags. Feed every flag into tactic.md — and never back into the judge. The judge absorbs nothing; the tactic absorbs everything and visibly thickens.
00:22 · round two
Re-run the draft with the thicker tactic, grade it against the byte-identical judge. If round two beats round one against a judge that did not move, you've felt the loop — not believed in it, felt it.
00:30 · carry
Three markdown files, two sessions, about thirty minutes. You keep the round-by-round trail — the score, what the judge kept catching — so you walk into the make-this-a-team-check conversation holding a score trail, not a pitch.
Refuse the kind advice

The fast-iteration playbook will tell you to co-evolve: sharpen the work and sharpen the rubric together each round, "as your taste develops." Refuse it. A standard you are allowed to amend mid-run is not a standard — it is a mood. The moment judge.md is editable by the same hand that wants the score to go up, the grade is worthless: you have co-authored the verdict with the defendant.

And do not soften the rule when a round disappoints and the obvious fix is to relax one criterion. Ask the loop instead: "which rule did you claim to remove but actually kept under another name? Quote both lines." If generation could secretly edit the judge, that question has nowhere honest to land. If your "improvement" came from loosening the judge, you didn't tighten the work — you moved the goalposts.

A yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick. The standard does not get a vote on its own grade.

Where this sits · personal → team → company

A fixed judge is the verification primitive a company's autonomy rests on. Alone it raises one person off the bottleneck; shared, it lets a team run the same standard unattended; and once your taste lives in a frozen judge.md that separate agents are scored against, quality stops being a person reviewing every output and becomes infrastructure the whole company can trust agent work against — one standard, not one desk at a time. That trust is the precondition everything above it composes on. It's the same shape the software lane calls verifier-shaped-to-failure: freeze the check, evolve the code — different surface, identical move.

The ledger · in one glance
What you built
A frozen judge.md, a separate generator agent, an evolving tactic.md, and the round-by-round trail of scores and tactic diffs. One file moves; one never does.
The integrity test
Ask the loop: "which rule did you claim to remove but actually kept under another name? Quote both lines." If generation could secretly edit the judge, that question has nowhere honest to land.
Monday move
Pick one output you sanity-check yourself. Write its standard as a one-page judge.md and resolve never to edit it this run. Three markdown files · two agent sessions · ~30 min · nothing to buy or clear first.
Verification
Recipe · shared lane · Verification → Absorption

Earn the next rung

The principle: Trust is earned, not granted — no benchmark proves an agent is reliable for YOUR process; only observed performance on your data does.

Turn every permission decision — let it act, or only propose? — into a ladder you climb one rung at a time, by building the check that would have caught the failure before you climb.

Rung 4 is boring — the failure mode fired in February, the check caught it, no drama. That's the condition for climbing.
The mechanism · the jump that breaks things

The gap isn't access. It's trust.

Almost every organisation with a working pilot has the same failure mode. The demo goes well, excitement builds, someone decides to skip the boring middle part and push the agent from "it drafts, we review" to "it acts, we check the logs." The problem is not the agent — it's that nobody has actually seen the failure mode in their data, their edge cases, their org's particular flavour of weird. The move from rung 1 to rung 5 in one leap is not bold. It's just skipping the evidence collection.

Across domains — legal, cross-industry, security, finance, software — the same pattern recurs widely enough to be beyond doubt: access to AI is high and rising; autonomous production trust lags far behind, and the gap is large and consistent everywhere it's been looked at. (The per-domain figures below come from different surveys, methods, and definitions of "autonomous" — so read the direction, which is unanimous, not the decimals.) This is not a slow adoption curve. It's an org-learning bottleneck. The bottleneck is not access. It is the absence of a protocol for building observed competence between pilot and deploy. The autonomy ladder is that protocol, made explicit and auditable.

No governance platform can grant trust. No vendor benchmark proves an agent is reliable for YOUR process. Trust is earned the same way it is between humans: observed performance, over time, in your context.

Process diagram · 01The ladder is directional: each rung earned gives you the observed evidence to authorise the next one. Rungs 5 and 6 are receded — you don't grant them, you build toward them.
The rung-climb protocol · what "earned" means exactly

Run the proposal version first.

Before any rung promotion, run the agent in proposal mode at the new rung — it produces exactly what it would do, you observe it, you don't apply it. This is not risk-aversion theatre. It is the only way to see the failure mode in your data, not the vendor's benchmark. Vendor benchmarks are measured on the vendor's test set. Your calendar, your Slack history, your ticket queue, your customers' edge cases — these are not in the test set. The failure mode in your context only becomes visible when you run your context.

The rung is earned when three conditions hold simultaneously: (1) the proposal version passed N times with no surprise — N higher for higher blast radius; (2) the failure mode now has an explicit functioning check — the bad version would have been caught; (3) that check has fired at least once on real input. Not conceptually. Actually fired. Elapsed time is not a condition. Vendor confidence scores are not a condition. The check firing on real input is the condition.

The check that catches the failure is not overhead. It is the durable institutional artefact. The next engineer who inherits the deployment doesn't just get an agent — they get a trust map that shows which rungs have been earned, what check is in place at each one, and when it last fired. That's the difference between tribal knowledge and a transferable operating model.

Process diagram · 02Each climb produces a check, not just confidence. The check is the durable artefact — the institutional memory of where this agent fails in your context.
The artefact · what the check actually is

The failure mode is the specification.

Designing the check that would have caught the failure is not a defensive move. It is the moment you understand the agent well enough to give it more autonomy. The check encodes your accumulated knowledge of where the agent fails on your specific process. An agent without checks isn't "low overhead." It's just an agent whose failure modes haven't been documented yet.

The check needs to be concrete and executable, not a policy statement. "Review high-stakes emails" is not a check — it's a thought you had once. A check is something that runs: a judge that flags sentiment drift, a classifier that catches blast radius, a simple rule that blocks actions touching more than N records. The criterion is equally simple: would this check have caught the bad version, reliably? If yes, you have a check. If the answer is "probably," you have a hypothesis that needs to fire on real input before it earns that status.

Process diagram · 03Template — adapt to your risk profile. ⚠ not a researched norm The month-by-month percentages are a single-source practitioner scaffold — useful as a planning starting point; your sequence depends on your observed failure modes and blast radius.
What "boring" means in practice

The goal is a boring check.

"Boring" is the operational test for rung advancement. Not "the agent did well this week." Not "we're comfortable." Boring means: the check fires, catches the bad version, and nobody is surprised. The failure mode has become a known quantity. It appears, the check catches it, you log it, you move on. The anxiety around "what if it does something wrong?" has been replaced by a specific, answerable question: "did the check fire today?"

This matters especially at the transition from rung 3 to rung 4 — from proposal to action. That's the rung where the agent stops asking and starts doing. The temptation is to reason about it in the abstract: "the blast radius is low, the actions are reversible, we're comfortable." The discipline is to run the proposal version N times until the boring condition holds, then flip the switch. The difference between these two paths, at scale, across a dozen agents, is the difference between an org that owns its AI deployment and one that hopes for the best.

The ceiling in the planning template — call it 95%, though it's an illustrative template number and yours will differ — is worth noting only for what it isn't: it's never 100%. Not because the remaining few percent will inevitably fail, but because architecture that assumes 100% trust is architecture that has stopped watching. Rung 6 — escalate the rest — is always on. That's not a limitation. That's the design.

Use when

You have a working agent and a permission decision: let it act, or only propose? This question recurs at every new scope — new connector, new action type, new team, new blast radius. The temptation is to jump because the demo went well. The risk is you haven't seen the failure mode in your data yet.

Build

A per-deployment trust/permission map — one table per agent: Rung · Action class · Current status · Check in place · N clean runs · Blocker to next rung. Makes the current rung visible to the next engineer, compliance, quarterly review.

Test

Three conditions simultaneously: proposal passed N times; failure mode has a functioning check; check fired on real input. Not elapsed time. Not vendor benchmarks. Observed competence on your process.

Core moves

How a rung gets earned

The protocol, not the permission.
1

Name the current rung

Honestly. Most agents are rung 1 or 2. The map starts here.

2

Run proposal mode at next rung

See what it would do. Don't apply it yet. See the failure mode in your data.

3

Design the check

The bad version would have been caught by: ___. Write that sentence. Make it executable.

4

Let the check fire

On real input. Not conceptually. At least once. Now you have evidence.

5

Reach boring

N clean runs, no surprises. The check fires, catches it, nobody panics.

6

Advance the rung

Update the trust map. The check stays. It is now institutional memory.

proposal runs→failure surfaces→check designed→boring→rung advanced

Then repeat at the next rung. Each climb leaves a check: compound institutional knowledge of where this agent fails in your context.
