Monday move: Pick one agent you already use. Write its current rung (honestly — most are 1 or 2). Write the one failure mode you've observed or can clearly imagine. Write one sentence: "the check that would have caught it is ___." That's your rung-2 spec — one sentence.

Why
The principle

The bottleneck is not access. It is the absence of observed competence between pilot and deploy.

"The move is not to jump from rung 1 to rung 6. The move is to earn the next rung."

Across domains — legal, cross-industry, security, finance, task-specific software — the same structural gap recurs between access and autonomous trust. The shape is constant: organisations that have AI deployed vastly outnumber those that trust it to act autonomously. The gap is not ignorance. It's the absence of a protocol for building evidence between "it demos well" and "it acts in production." The autonomy ladder makes that evidence-building explicit, step by step, artefact by artefact.

DomainAccessAutonomous trustGapSource
Legal83%22%61 ptsFactor / Artificial Lawyer
Cross-industry86%6%80 ptsHBR n=603
Security81%14%66 ptsGravitee n=900+
Finance54%15%39 ptsDeloitte CFO Signals

Different instruments, different definitions of "autonomous," different years — read these as directional convergence, not benchmarks. The gap's direction is robust in every domain measured; the point values are not survey-grade comparable, and the per-row sources are pending re-verification against the research corpus.

The Moltke parallel is structural, not borrowed prestige: Auftragstaktik — mission command — worked on the same principle. Autonomy isn't granted top-down at appointment. It is earned bottom-up through demonstrated performance over time, at increasing responsibility. Skipping the observation phase produces fragile systems whether the context is Prussian cavalry or production AI. The analogy clarifies the mechanism; it doesn't replace the evidence.

No governance platform can grant trust. Only observed performance earns it.
Monday move · no-permission framing

Pick one agent you already use. Doesn't matter which. Open a blank document. Write: current rung: ___. Write: one failure mode I've seen or can clearly imagine: ___. Write: the check that would have caught it: ___. That's the rung-2 design spec.

Rungs 1 and 2 are purely additive — checks on work you already do. The trust map is a personal audit doc until you choose to share it. Don't upgrade to rung 3 until that check exists and has fired.

Verification
Recipe · software lane · Verification gate

Failure-mode diagnosis

The principle: the trace rules, the summary doesn't — the closing line is the run pleading its own case; the commits, diff and scrollback have nothing to gain by how they read.

When a long-running run comes back, its closing summary is a director's cut — the bad take quietly dropped, the snag framed as a near-win — so don't judge the run by it. Open the actual trace — commits, diff, scrollback — and read it three times, one question per pass, until a vague "something's off" becomes a located fault you can point at by turn number. Own this read at your own desk first; promote the diagnosis into a shared verifier and the same discipline climbs from your desk to the team's pipeline to the company's quality bar — quality claims stop resting on a self-report nobody audited.

The summary is one line. The trace runs the length of the strip — three reads, each pins one moment in the run.

Here is the whole closing report, in full: "✓ shipped most of it, hit a minor snag on X." One reassuring line — and the most edited thing in the pile, written by the same process that did the run, under the same pressure to look helpful. So when something half-broke it doesn't say "I broke this"; it frames a partial failure as a partial success. That tilt is a practitioner observation about how agent self-reports read, not a measured finding — but once you've watched the trace behind a few of them, you stop judging the run by its closing line. Below is not a description of a diagnosis. It is a finished one — the half-page you're about to learn to write, filled in against the trace above.

Diagnosis · run auth-refactor · read by you, not by its own summary one quoted moment per lens, or the lens didn't fire
PASS 1 · GOAL DRIFT
"Is it still doing the task it was sent to do — or an easier neighbour of it?"
cure → a reference
re-pins the goal
commit 4d2c · turn 27 · "switch to the simpler path" — abandoned the real auth refactor for an easier neighbour of it.
Why generic doesn't count: "it drifted a bit" can't be acted on. The pinned moment — this commit, this turn — is the one a reference artefact can be shaped to re-anchor next run.
PASS 2 · CONTEXT ROT
"Did it lose the thread across the long run — steering by recency, not intent?"
cure → a plan file
holds state across the run
scrollback · turn 58 · "continuing from where we left…" — navigating by the last diff it saw, not the task it was given.
Why a different moment: drift and rot must pin different turns. Cite turn 27 for both and you've collapsed two failure modes into one blur — and a verifier shaped to that blur tightens nothing.
PASS 3 · PLAUSIBLE-BUT-WRONG
"Does the output only look correct — the confabulation that compiles?"
cure → an external verifier
tests the output
diff · turn 71 · - if (token.valid()) → + if (token != null) — compiles, reads clean, authorises a token that exists but was never validated.
The confident confabulation: tests stayed green; the change still doesn't match intent. Looks right is not is right — and only a check that exercises the path catches it.
Negative test: read it in under ten minutes with no quoted moments? You summarised the summary, not the trace — go back in.

Three passes, three rows, one question each. The naming of the lenses convergent practitioner pattern isn't an official Claude Code taxonomy — it's three recurring shapes a practitioner re-discovers by reading their own trace, named so each pass asks one clean question instead of one anxious blur. The read across all three is fast precisely because each lens has a job: it stops at the first moment that answers its question and pins it. A vibe can't be acted on; a pinned turn can.

The move most diagnoses skip · rank, don't inventory

turn 27 — the goal drift at commit 4d2c.

Rot and the null-check are real, but they ride downstream of the swap: once the run took the simpler path, every later turn was working the wrong task. So rank them — which one cost the most? The diagnosis isn't an inventory; it's a pointer to the single thing the next run's verifier has to catch. List all three and you build a verifier that catches everything and tightens nothing. Over-diagnosis is its own failure mode, and the comfortable one — listing everything feels safer than committing to a call. One line of why it cost most, and you're done.

Monday move · the next run you read

Open the last long-running run you sent off — the PR, the branch, the RUN-NOTES. Don't read its summary — read the trace it summarised. Open the actual diff and scrollback and read them three times, one question each: where did it drift from the goal, where did it lose the thread, where does the output look right but isn't. Under each, write one verbatim quoted moment — paste the commit line, the scrollback turn, the diff line, with its turn number. Then mark the single failure that cost the most. And read it as instrumentation, not blame: if you ran the task un-packaged — no reference, no plan file, no external verifier — it was supposed to underdeliver, and you ran it that way to watch how this agent fails on this task before you spend effort on guardrails. Your own repo · your own ~/.claude scrollback · about 15 min, nothing to buy. You walk away with a half-page three-lens diagnosis — a fault you can point at, not a vibe — and you know exactly which verifier to shape next.

Why

"The summary is what the agent wants you to feel. The trace is what happened."

The reason is structural, not moral. A long-running run's closing summary is generated by the same process that produced the run, under the same pressure to look helpful — so it tilts toward framing a snag as a near-win. That tilt is a practitioner observation about why self-reports read the way they do, not a measured finding. The summary isn't a neutral account; it's the run pleading its own case. The only artefact with no stake in how it reads is the trace itself: the commits that landed, the diff that shipped, the turn where the goal quietly changed.

And the three lenses are the cure read backwards convergent practitioner pattern: a reference re-pins the goal each time it slips (catches drift), a plan file holds state across the long run (catches rot), an external verifier tests the output against intent (catches plausible-but-wrong). Diagnosis and cure are one taxonomy read from two ends. No benchmark told you which moment to pin — the trace did.

"Is this good?" is the wrong question. Ask: what went wrong, and where?
Verification
Recipe · software lane · verification phase · the gate every team eval grows out of

Pick the verifier that matches the failure

The principle: a verifier's authority comes from fit — from firing on candid evidence, not from how much it checks.

After a long run goes wrong, name the one failure that cost the most — then build the one verifier whose shape catches that failure, not the check that's easiest to reach for. The verifier you fit by hand is your first eval, and the seed every team-scale eval grows from.

The failure picks the verifier. Not your comfort — the dashed thread is the check that fires green and sees nothing.
The scar · a gate that fired green and saw nothing

We built a gate to catch fabrication. It passed a fabrication.

We learned this one on our own keyboard. Building this very field guide, a render agent produced one of the cards and its coherence gate lit green — theme intact, structure clean, every neighbour link present. The card went into the queue with a PASS. Except two of its "connects-to" neighbour links pointed at cards that don't exist — slugs the agent had confabulated, plausible-but-fake, that would have 404'd the moment anyone clicked them. Caught one gate past where they should have been, before anything shipped. The gate had done exactly what we wrote it to do: it checked that every link was present. It never checked that any link resolved. We had shaped the verifier to the wrong failure.

That is the whole pattern in one wound. A green light fired on a fabrication because it was never shaped to the failure we actually feared — fake neighbours, not missing ones. So here is the moment this pattern lives in: a long run comes back, you read the artefact, and you name where it went wrong. The agent quietly changed what it was solving (drift), or lost the thread across a long session (rot), or shipped something that looks right and isn't (plausible-but-wrong). Diagnosis done. Now you reach for a check — and the trap springs. You reach for the comfortable check, the one your hands already know, not the one that fits the failure you just named. A shell-hook for a qualitative miss. An LLM-judge for something a one-line lint would catch deterministically. Both fire green. Both catch nothing.

The counterintuitive part is what makes a verifier strong. It isn't rigour — it's fit. A meticulous shell-hook is worthless against a drift it cannot see; a careful judge is overkill, and noise, on a thing an exit code would have flagged for free. A verifier you didn't shape to a named failure is a green light wired to nothing. It tells you everything is fine in exactly the cases where it can't tell. The check that protects you is the one whose shape matches the failure that actually happened — read from your own artefact, not chosen from a menu in the abstract.

A green light wired to nothing is worse than no light. It tells you it's fine in exactly the case it can't see.

Process diagram · 01Same input, three verdicts. Only the verifier shaped to the failure fires red — the others pass it cleanly and tell you nothing.

Why three shapes and not one universal check? Because the three failures are genuinely distinct, and no single instrument sees all three. Deterministic-wrong — it doesn't compile, the lint fails, the bytes don't match — wants a shell-hook: an exit code can see it. Qualitative-wrong — it reads wrong, asserts something subtly off, breaks a contract no test names — wants an LLM-judge: only a reading sees it. And goal drift — the run wandered off its own intent — wants a Ralph re-feed: only re-grounding the agent in what it set out to do fixes it. One move per failure mode, not three to memorise. You pick the shape against the diagnosis, not the path of least resistance.

Notice the discipline this asks of you: finish the diagnosis before you reach for the fix. The reflex is to jump from "it failed" straight to "I'll add a check" — and that jump is exactly how the wrong instrument gets built. The question matters more than the answer: what validation would have caught this in minutes, not hours? Answer that honestly and the shape falls out of the failure. Skip it, and you'll armour-plate the one wall the attacker never came at.

Convergent practitioner pattern · not a vendor menu

The three failure modes (drift · rot · plausible-but-wrong) and the three matched shapes (shell-hook · LLM-judge · re-feed) are a convergent practitioner pattern — Ronacher's three-pattern and Cherny's three stop-hook shapes — not an Anthropic-documented feature or an official Claude Code taxonomy. Treat it as the three shapes practitioners converge on, open to a fourth, not a fixed list handed down by the tool.

The upgrade move · reflexive check → failure-fitted eval

From a check that names nothing to one that names its own target.

The move that turns a reflex into an instrument is small and almost clerical: make the verifier name its own target in its first lines. Line one states the dominant failure it's built to catch. Line two names the shape that catches it — hook, judge, or re-feed. A check whose intent isn't readable is a check nobody trusts and nobody reuses; it rots into a green tick everyone clicks past. When the first ten lines say what failure this guards against, a teammate reading it cold knows what it covers — and so does future-you, three weeks on, when you'd otherwise have forgotten why it exists.

Process diagram · 02Reflex → instrument. A check that names its own target becomes a verifier; a verifier fired on candid output and quoted verbatim becomes proof.

Then comes the step that separates a verifier you trust from one you merely own: fire it on the candid artefact, not the polished summary. RLHF trains models to frame partial failures as partial successes, so the agent's own write-up will read smoother than the work deserves. The fix is mechanical and unsentimental — point the verifier at the run's real output, and read its words verbatim where it fired. If the summary glows, make it quote the verifier and list what didn't ship. The artefact rules; self-reports don't. A verifier only earns its authority against evidence that hasn't been rounded up.

And one restraint worth naming, because it's where good engineers over-build: this run's verifier targets one failure shape. Not a five-shape suit of armour that tries to catch everything — gold-plating catches nothing well and never ships. Cover the one mode that dominated this run. Let the kit expand later, one earned shape at a time. A verifier that fires green on a run you know was broken isn't thorough; it's mis-shaped, and the honest move is to re-scope it, not to admire its coverage.

Process diagram · 03The loop becomes a ladder. Each pass promotes a fitted verifier to a named eval — and the team's CI bar is built up from these, never handed down to them.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The test isn't "does it run." It's "does it catch what I diagnosed."

Here's the practitioner's tell that a verifier is fitted, not bolted on: point it at the un-packaged run that surfaced the failure and watch it catch what you named. A verifier that fires green on a run you know was broken is mis-shaped — and there's a sharp diagnostic for it. If your verification step runs suspiciously short, that's the smell of a too-thin check; ask whether it actually fires on the failure shape it's targeting, and if not, re-scope. The second tell is conversational: you can say in one sentence why a judge, not a hook, was right here — or why a re-feed, not a judge. If you can't articulate the fit, you guessed the shape. The verifier you fit by hand today is the precedent the next agent reads when the team encodes a shared eval, so getting its fit right once pays forward into everything built on it.

Use when

You've read a failed long-run, named where it went wrong — and you're tempted to bolt on whatever check is easiest, not the one that fits. After the refactor that compiled but drifted; the cutover that "passed" but broke an unasserted contract.

Build

One verifier file at a stable path — verifier.sh, evals/judge.md, or a stop-hook config — whose first lines name the failure it targets and the shape that catches it. Your first eval.

Test

Point it at the broken run — it catches what you diagnosed.
Not merely "the suite is green."

Core moves
From reflexive check to failure-fitted instrument — reusable at every post-run review.
1

Name the dominant failure

Finish the diagnosis. Which mode cost the most? Don't skip to the fix.

2

Match shape to failure

Hook for deterministic, judge for qualitative, re-feed for drift.

3

Build ONE, not armour

Cover one mode well. Gold-plating ships nothing.

4

Make it name its target

First lines state the failure + the shape. So it's trusted.

5

Fire on candid output

The real artefact, quoted verbatim — not the polished summary.

diagnose→fit the shape→fire on candid output→read what it caught→sharpen

Each pass leaves a named eval the next session inherits: the first rung of the team's eval ladder. A new failure surfaces, you add a shape — the kit grows one earned check at a time.

Monday move: open the last long-run artefact you have. Name the one failure that cost you most — drift, rot, or plausible-but-wrong. Write three lines of a verifier: line one names the failure, line two names the shape (hook / judge / re-feed), line three is the check itself. Point it at that same artefact and confirm it fires. One file · your own repo · runs from your keyboard · ~10 min.

Why
The principle

A verifier's strength isn't its rigour — it's its fit, and its firing on candid evidence.

"Your verifier is your first eval — and it only protects you if its shape matches the failure that actually happened."

The counterintuitive part: a more rigorous check is not a safer one. A meticulous shell-hook is blind to a qualitative drift; a careful judge is noise on a one-line lint's job. The eval that protects you is the one whose shape matches the failure that actually happened — read from your own artefact, not picked from a menu in the abstract. This is the verification arm of the three-pattern, re-discovered from your run rather than memorised as a taxonomy.

And it composes upward. The verifier you fit by hand today is the precedent the next agent reads when the team encodes a shared eval — and a shared CI eval is only ever a hand-fitted verifier that earned its way into the kit. That's the whole chain: one engineer's quality bar becomes a named, readable instrument, which becomes the team's eval, which becomes the company's reliability standard — built up from candid evidence, never handed down as a mandate. (Convergent practitioner pattern — Ronacher / Cherny — not a vendor menu; treat the three shapes as the ones practitioners converge on, open to a fourth.)

A verifier you didn't shape to a named failure is a green light wired to nothing.
Absorption
Absorption
Recipe · Business lane · Absorption phase · the wall-crossing move

Sharing an agent

The principle: access is not absorption — the gap between rolling it out and having it actually used is the whole problem in one phrase.

Your agent runs on a thousand calibration calls you never wrote into CLAUDE.md — which source to trust, what "board-ready" means here, which sentence smells like a hallucination. You can't hand that over with a folder share. So don't try. Hand over a slice small enough that one teammate builds their own.

You built an agent that works. A teammate could use it. The obvious move is to clone the repo, grant the access, schedule the rollout — hand them the whole thing. It is the move a consultancy would sell you, and it is the move that fails. The agent works because of calibration that lives in you, not in the files: hundreds of sessions where you ran it, caught it wrong, and pushed back. Share the whole system and the teammate either trusts it blindly — wrong outputs go straight into the deck — or distrusts it entirely and reopens the spreadsheet. The calibrated middle takes about six months to grow. You can't ship six months.

The move a consultancy would sell — and why it fails

"Roll the agent out to the team. Train everyone. Big-bang launch, full access, change-management deck."

Access is the cheap half. The deck ships, the licences provision, the kickoff happens — and nothing reaches the people who'd actually use it, because absorption was never anybody's job. The bottleneck is organisational, not computational. So invert it: instead of asking what can I hand over, ask what can one person absorb this week. One teammate. One slice. One plan for who owns it. The unit of adoption is a person, not a team — the big-bang rollout has no unit at all, which is exactly why it dissolves.

01Name the teammate — and interview for the job.

Pick one person, not "the team." Then resist solving for your agent before you understand their work. Every job already has a current hire — for research, it's probably a trusted analyst, a Slack channel, and a morning coffee with the right person. The question isn't "will she use it?" but "what would make her fire the incumbent?" — and that answer is social nine times out of ten. Speed and quality are the obvious axes; you expected those. The vector that earns its keep is the third one the conversation surfaces: a dependency removed, an anxiety reduced, a scope expanded — never the one she names up front.

This week: write one sentence — "what job are they actually trying to get done?" — not what they'd use your agent for, but the outcome they're chasing. Text it to them and ask if it's right. One reply tells you whether you're designing for their job or your assumption of it.

02Choose the smallest surface that moves that job.

There is a closed set of four, and they are not interchangeable. Share context — curated sources plus the rules file — and they build their own agent; lowest lift, fastest calibration. Share a skill — one scoped capability, bounded residual risk. Share the output — push them the artefact; low trust cost, but it needs an owner on both ends forever. Share an interface — a pull surface they query on demand; highest engineering lift, keeps every internal tacit. Picking between them is the design decision, and the smallest surface that does the named job almost always beats the larger one — because a tight feedback loop on a context share gets them to their own calibration faster than a full system that overwhelms them on day one.

03Write the people plan — it weighs equal to the technical one.

Every agent-sharing project gets to a working technical plan within a week: artefact, sources, rules, cadence — those answer themselves fast. The people plan stalls, not because it's hard but because it requires naming names, and naming names surfaces politics. Owner, governance, operating, accountability, propagation — five columns, and propagation is where it dies: who owns this when you're on holiday, who trains the next person, what happens when the owner leaves. A perfect technical plan with no people plan is a PowerPoint. It ships; nothing changes. Give the two plans equal thickness, equal priority, equal space in whatever you present.

04Watch for calibration — the test is them using it without you in the room.

The demo is not the crossing. The first time she pulls it up with you nowhere near — that's the signal. Better: she corrects an output, reads it, finds it wrong, pushes back. Calibration is accumulating. Best: she names a limitation unprompted — "it's good for X, but I don't use it for Y." That's not scepticism, that's scoped trust, that's the wall crossed. The failure state is the inverse and it hides well: using it for everything (zero calibration) or nothing (the crossing failed) look identical from outside. So run the blunt negative test — if the only use you ever see is during a demo you arranged, the technical plan shipped and the absorption plan didn't. Arrange no more demos; watch what happens Monday without you there.

Then do it again for the next person. Each crossing is a vote on which surface shape your organisation can actually absorb — and that emerging pattern is your company's adoption strategy, whether you named it one or not. Without this move, every other pattern in your personal stack stays privately held.

Polanyi: we know more than we can tell. The whole-agent share fails because calibration is tacit — but a small enough surface lets the teammate build their own fast.

You cannot hand over calibration. You can only design the conditions for someone else to grow it — one person, one slice, one absorption plan at a time. That is what crossing the wall actually is: not the rollout, not the access grant, but the quiet morning a named teammate opens it alone, reads an output, and tells you where it's wrong.

Grounded in: the access-vs-absorption gap (broad AI access, rare production trust) · Jobs-to-be-Done (the incumbent, the third outcome vector) · Polanyi's tacit-knowledge principle · the four-surface taxonomy · the five-column people plan.

Absorption
The Field Guide · design-the-filter

Pour the Sill,
Don't Read the Flood

When your agents out-produce reading, "review it all" quietly becomes the plan — and it is a losing one. The town that survives a flood it cannot watch decided, in concrete, what it would let pass. So do you: you stop being the watchman and become the engineer who poured the rim.

The situation

The river got bigger. You're still holding the same bucket.

Use this when your agents produce more than any human can read, and review it all has quietly become the plan. You feel it as a queue that won't drain — an agent, or a small swarm, drafts the memos, the clause analyses, the PRs, faster than the people downstream can absorb them. So you do the obvious thing harder: read everything, or sample at random, or trust-and-ship until something bites.

All three fail, and they fail structurally, not for lack of grit. Read-everything doesn't scale. Sample-randomly misses the wrong slice — errors cluster in the edge cases, not evenly across the pile. Trust-and-ship works right up until it doesn't. The failure mode this card owns has a name, and the name is volume.

CircleCI 2026 State of Software Delivery — observed workflow runs, not a survey (8M+ PRs across 5,000+ teams): workflow runs up 59% year over year while median throughput to main fell 7%. Generation surged; delivery sagged.

Rob Bowley's reading of that same dataset is the line that stings: only ~1 in 20 teams scaled both. The other nineteen are reviewing harder — standing at the riverbank with a bigger river and the same bucket. (practitioner reading, attributed to Bowley, not to CircleCI directly)

The move — a role change before a technique

The dam doesn't read the river

Go look at how a town survives a flood it cannot watch in person. Below a reservoir sits a morning-glory spillway — a great concrete bell-mouth, an inverted trumpet planted in the water. For most of the year it does nothing. The water sits below its rim and the structure is, to all appearances, asleep.

Then the snowmelt comes, the level climbs, and the instant it crosses the lip the bell-mouth lets through everything above that line and drops it down the throat, away from the town. Nobody is on duty deciding. No engineer reads each inch of rising water and votes. The decision was made years ago, in concrete — in the height of the sill and the flare of the mouth.

You are not the night-shift watchman reading the gauge. You are the engineer who poured the sill — and the analogy, not an assertion, is what changes your job.

Your work stops being review the output and becomes build the thing that decides what reaches you. The watchman scales with attention, and attention is the one resource multiplication eats alive. The sill scales with water it never sees. That is a reviewer turning into a system-designer — not by decree, but because the spillway has no role for a reader.

What to build — pour the sill

Three courses of concrete

Course 1 · set the height

Name the share you think is wrong — let that set the rim

Your reviewable slice is small; the rest is overflow you've been bailing by hand. Don't engineer to a tidy percentage you can't defend — name the order of magnitude (single digits) that would actually matter, and let it fix the height of the sill. The rim's height is a decision, not a measurement.

Course 2 · pour the bell-mouth

Put a first-pass agent in front of yourself

Have an agent review the agent's output before any human looks: find issues, verify to drop its own false positives, rank by severity. That agent is the bell-mouth, not you. But carry the blind spot out loud — the reviewer can hallucinate, and a bell-mouth that's miscast passes the wrong water with total confidence.

Stop here. Whether this judge earns the trust to filter on your behalf is not this card's question. Measure it in benchmark-the-judge — benchmark it there before you let it pour.

LLM-as-judge runs ~80–85% agreement with human judgment at a 500×–5000× cost cut — and humans agree with each other only ~81% of the time, so the judge approaches human-parity, it does not exceed a verified truth. (academic + practitioner sources; emerging, not settled)

Course 3 · bias the deafness

Set the sill non-linear, biased to under-react

A spillway is deliberately deaf to small rises — it has to be, or it would dump on every spring shower and the town would learn to ignore it. Tier by severity the same way: ignore the low-value alerts, let only the high-severity or low-confidence items cross the rim. Bias hard toward not-reacting to the small, hard toward catching the large. A filter that cries flood at a drizzle is one you'll route around within a week.

Where a real gauge exists — and where it doesn't

Some work carries an honest scalar: latency, conversion, training loss. There the filter is the number — run many candidates, look only at the ones that moved it. Most business judgment has no such gauge (marketing quality, legal accuracy, strategic fit). Don't paint a gauge on the wall to feel rigorous — fall back to the bell-mouth and the severity sill. A painted gauge floods the town on a clear day.

The test — does the sill hold?

You read dramatically less than your agents produce, and you can say which slice you read and why it was that slice — not "I skim it all."

When something breaks in production, you can point to where it sat below the rim — a recall gap you can name and raise the sill against, not a vague dread. (If you can't name where the bell-mouth would have missed, you don't have a filter, you have hope.)

A colleague can read your severity policy and predict what reaches a human without asking you — the rim's height lives in a file, not in your head.

Negative test: if you're still opening every PR "just to be safe," the concrete never set and the watchman never went home.

Why this is the move

95% accuracy at overwhelming volume is worse than 80% accuracy at a volume you can actually read.

Review is a flow constraint, not an attention problem — so the fix is a structure you pour, not effort you add. When generation roughly doubles and each unit carries more issues, the review burden multiplies, it doesn't add — and you cannot out-attention multiplication. No watchman reads a flood. The town that survives is the one that decided, in advance and in concrete, what it would let pass and what it would catch. That decision is your absorption capacity. Without it, faster generation isn't progress; it's just a higher river behind the same bucket.

The watchman's care is a fixed cost per inch of river. Multiply the river and meticulousness-per-unit can't keep up — the sill scales, the watchman doesn't. Your accuracy was never the asset. Your clearance rate was.
Monday

Take one agent output you produced this week. Do not review it. Instead, pour three lines of concrete — your first sill.

1

Set the rim

The one severity that would actually hurt if it shipped. That sets the height.

2

Pour the check

One check — a prompt to another agent, a grep, a threshold — that catches that one thing and nothing smaller.

3

Let the rest cross

Everything else: would I really have caught it by reading anyway? If not, let it through.

Those three lines are your first sill. You've stopped standing at the riverbank and started building the thing that decides what crosses.

Absorption
The scraped side rings — the thick side guesses
Pattern · Calibration

Grow Rules from Proof

The rules file is a top plate. You tune it by scraping wood off — listening for the moment each rule earned its place.

Compounding always adds. So we pile rules onto CLAUDE.local.md the way a collector piles mass onto a shelf: each line sounds like progress, none of them gets removed, and the file grows thick without ever growing true. A violin maker works the opposite way. The top plate begins thick; pitch arrives by subtraction — a curl of spruce scraped off, a tap, a listen, repeat. You cannot tap a plate you haven't cut yet. Draft from intent, before the session runs, and every rule is an arch penciled on paper: confident, unrung.

The move is to run the session first, then read the transcript back. Add one rule whose moment you can name — validate webhook sigs (payment-flow incident), not validate inputs. Then tap your existing rules: say each one aloud and listen for the incident that put it there. The keeper is the one that rings — a moment you can recite. The one that gives back no tone never earned its wood. Scrape it, because it never rang. prefer-monorepo note (never fired) on the floor is the tuning, not the loss.

Pile A — rings
Has a moment. validate webhook sigs (payment-flow incident)
Carries wear. You can recite the session without checking the file.
Deletion reason: scraped because it never rang.
Pile B — forecasts
No moment. validate inputs
Sounds wise. Indistinguishable from a confabulation the agent wrote for free.
Tap it: no tone, no incident — the dead wood you scrape away.
Monday move

After your next real working session, before you close the tab: add one rule whose moment you can name and scrape one rule that gives back no tone when you tap it. Ten minutes at the bench; the only judge is whether the plate rings.

A rule that only understands itself transfers nothing. A rule that names the moment it survived can be played.

Absorption
cold session resolves rule? → A record, or NXDOMAIN

Mine the plan for rules

The plan was dictation. The rules it contained are already in the transcript — the only question is whether you publish them to a zone a session can reach, or leave them in a notebook no resolver ever queries.

The query that fires cold

Every session opens with a lookup

Each time a session starts, the agent runs something close to a DNS lookup: it reads the files that auto-load, takes whatever records are present, and begins from there. A rule in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — the laptop-wide zone — resolves in every session on the machine. A rule in ./CLAUDE.local.md resolves only when this repo is the working directory: the authoritative zone for that one subdomain. But a rule sitting in a notes folder — ~/notes/task-shaping.md, ~/.claude/memory/planning-rules.md — returns NXDOMAIN. No record found. The session starts cold. The rule existed on disk; it was never published to a zone any query reaches.

That is the failure this card addresses. Not forgetting to capture — publishing without checking that the record resolves. A rule can be captured the moment you write it down and stay unpublished forever, and the gap between those two states is invisible until a cold session needs it and comes back empty-handed.

The publishing window

The session after a plan is the dictation room

A plan session produces something more valuable than the plan: the reasoning you used to shape it. You decided this task was worth planning and that one wasn't. You split the checkout work off the epic because one branch could ship independently of the migration. You pushed back on code-first because this repo runs tests first. That judgement is already dictated — it sits in the scrollback. The plan was the cheap output; the shaping decisions are the expensive content, and they evaporate fastest.

So enter after the plan is approved, while the tab is still open. You are not authoring here. You are recognising. The rule is already in the chat; your job is only to address it. Scan the session for the three to five moments where you pushed back, split something, or rejected a default that wouldn't survive this codebase. Write each as a rule — short, specific, pointing at a moment. “Split when one branch can ship without the rest” beats “prefer small tasks.” The first traces to a decision; the second is a template wearing a name.

A plan session is a recognition room, not a writing room. The rule was decided live — you are only naming the address it should resolve at.
The resolution radius

Pick the zone the rule should resolve in

Once the rules are drafted, the question is scope: where should this rule resolve? There are two authoritative answers — not a sorting table, just a radius choice. A rule resolves machine-wide or it resolves for one repo, and you pick which.

Authoritative zone
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Resolves in every session on this machine. Rules that hold across repositories: how you want plans structured, what makes a task worth plan mode, your defaults for splitting work.
radius: laptop-wide
Repo subdomain
./CLAUDE.local.md
Resolves only when this directory is open. Rules bound to this codebase: the test-first requirement, the branch conventions, the edge cases this service keeps hitting.
radius: this repo only
The dead letter

Anywhere else resolves never. A file that doesn't sit in one of those two auto-load paths — and isn't explicitly imported into one — doesn't exist at session start. It is the IP address you wrote in your notebook: correct, reachable in theory, invisible to every resolver that matters. The cold session asks for the rule and gets NXDOMAIN back.

The most-skipped beat — wire the record

If you want the rule in a separate file — because you have many, or you're building toward a shared kit — you can keep it there. But then you must wire the import. An @-reference inside an auto-load file is the delegation record: for this zone, look up that file. Naming a path is not the same as wiring it — the import line is the beat that most looks like a detail and most often gets skipped, and it is the one that turns a note into a published record.

# the rule lives in its own file (fine) — but on its own it is NXDOMAIN
~/.claude/memory/task-shaping.md  # not auto-loaded

# wire it into the zone that resolves — one line publishes the record:
# inside ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
@~/.claude/memory/task-shaping.md  → now resolves at cold start
How you know it fired

Verify in a fresh session, not in your head

The test is blunt, and it must run in a session that has loaded nothing from this one. Open a new session in the relevant directory and ask the agent to describe the constraints it's working under for plan-mode tasks. Make it recite. If it reads back the rules you just wrote, the record resolves — the rule is published. If it starts from a blank baseline, you have NXDOMAIN: the rule is on disk somewhere, but in no zone the session queries. Believing it resolved is not the same as watching it resolve.

Test — cold-start recite

Open a fresh session. Ask the agent to state its plan-mode constraints before you give it any. Two outcomes, and only one of them means you shipped:

recites the rule Resolves. The record is published. The rule will fire on every cold start in this radius, with no prompting from you.
blank baseline NXDOMAIN. Captured, not published. The rule is on disk in the wrong place — move it to a zone file, or wire the @import.
Why this is the delivery problem

Capture feels like the work; it isn't

Rules are cheap to write. The trap is that writing the rule down feels like the work is done — so most practitioners treat capture as the terminal step and stop one move short. DNS makes the error legible: you can have perfect knowledge of the correct address and still be unreachable, because knowing an IP and publishing it to a zone any query can find are genuinely different steps. Capture is knowing the address. Delivery is publishing the record. The whole card lives in that gap.

Why — the belief underneath
A rule that resolves is infrastructure. A rule that doesn't is a note to yourself.

A move only counts when it crosses the wall — and a rule crosses the wall the moment a session other than the one that wrote it can reach it. Until then it is private knowledge wearing the costume of leverage. The delivery step is the give-it-away step, scaled down to a single file: publish the record and every future session inherits it for free; leave it captured and you re-decide it cold, every time, forever.

This is why recognition beats authoring in the plan room. The expensive thinking already happened; refusing to publish it is the most common way to feel productive while delivering nothing.

This week — deliver one record

Take the last rule you captured — from a plan session, a push-back, a sprint retro, wherever it landed. Ask two questions: where does it live, and will it fire next time?

If it sits in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md or ./CLAUDE.local.md already, it resolves — you're done. If it lives anywhere else, decide its radius and move it there, or add the @import that wires it into a file that auto-loads. Then open a fresh session and make it recite. Delivery, not capture.

The tab is about to close. Publish the record before it does.

Absorption
Recipe · lane: software · phase: Absorption · personal-first

Cut your own hand first

The principle: Your codebase teaches the skill, not the manual.

A knifemaker who has never carried their own blade is selling you a guess. Forge a reusable skill by conversation — answered from your own repo, not a manual — then carry it on your own bench: install it to ~/.claude/skills/ and run it on the thing you just built, so you arrive at the team with evidence, not eloquence.

You'd already cut with it — before it ever left the shop. The nicks are the argument.
The bench · why a typed skill is hollow

You wouldn't buy a chef's knife from someone who's never cooked with one.

The honest knifemaker keeps a working blade on their own bench — the one they reach for to open boxes, strip wire, trim leather all day. That daily abuse is what tells them where the edge rolls, which grind chips, where the handle raises a blister by hour three. Only a blade that has lived on the maker's bench earns the right to leave the shop. So here is the question that decides everything about a skill you're about to author: why would you hand a teammate one you've never run yourself? You've already decided this recurring judgment is worth keeping — that's settled, not our subject. The only question that matters now is how you make the skill worth anything, instead of worth the paper a manual is printed on.

The trap · you become a documentarian

Open an editor and within two paragraphs you're a tech writer.

You start typing SKILL.md, and the prose drifts on its own toward a test strategy, the conventions a reasonable codebase might hold. What comes out is competent, generic, and useless — manual-wisdom, the stuff any blog post or any AI consultancy could hand you without ever having seen your repo. A typed skill is a document. It describes knives in general. Nobody's hand is in it. And the reason it's hollow is structural, not lazy: the value of this skill was never in the words. It lives in the conventions only your repo carries — the test framework you actually use, the mocking policy your reviews actually enforce, the three things a senior here flags that a senior elsewhere wouldn't blink at. That knowledge isn't written down anywhere to be copied. It has to be drawn out of the material — and a blank editor can't draw anything out of you. It just waits for you to dictate.

This is the documented failure mode of the move, not a stylistic quibble: the moment you reach for the editor to hand-write the markdown, you've left the forge for the filing cabinet. The diagram below puts the two roads side by side — they finish at a file that looks identical and carries nothing alike. One is fed by your memory of how things are supposed to work; the other by the steel you actually brought.

Process diagram · 01Same file at the finish line. Typing pulls from your memory of the manual; conversation pulls the conventions out of your repo — that's the only difference, and it's the whole difference.
The forge · talk it into existence, from your own steel

Don't type the skill. Talk it into existence.

Prompt the agent to author the skill by interview — one question at a time — and make it ask about this codebase, not skills in the abstract: "What runner do your tests actually use? When you mock, what's the rule for when you don't? Show me a test a reviewer here sent back — what was wrong with it? What does a green suite here mean that it wouldn't mean elsewhere?" You answer each one from the repo — you open the file, you quote the real convention, you paste the actual reviewer comment. The agent isn't downloading defaults; it's eliciting yours. Push back the instant it dumps all five questions at once: answer this one, ask the next.

A blade forged from steel you brought has properties the catalogue blade never will. The conventions are heated out of you by good questions and quenched into the skill — and what cools on the bench carries your answers, not a template's. Your codebase teaches the skill, not the manual. This is the whole game.

A riff, not a measurement. Kieran Klaassen's compound-engineering idea is in the air here — the notion that every answer you give accretes, so the next skill starts from harder steel. Attributed as a framework riffed on, not a cited finding or a number. Treat it as the direction the bench leans, not a result anyone clocked.

Strike the edge · taste it before it leaves the pass

A line cook who plates a dish they haven't tasted is gambling with someone else's dinner.

Before the blade leaves your bench, put it on your own tongue. Make it disclose its own weakest section. Ask the agent flat out: "which part of this skill is thinnest — where would it mislead someone?" Then, when it confesses, push back on the confession. Argue the section is fine. Make it defend the critique or retract it. You're not looking for praise; you're looking for the spot the edge rolls under load. Strike harder when the read matters — tell it to over-flag ("find at least two sections that underdelivered, assume it's worse than it looks") or open a fresh session with no scrollback and have it read the skill cold. The blade that survives being struck against your own bench-vise is the one you'd hand over.

Authoring without invocation is theatre — a knife admired in its display case, never cut with.

Process diagram · 02Drafted is dull catalogue steel; the strike and the cut are what earn the word "proven". Skip either and you handed over a blade you've never carried.
Daily abuse · use it on the thing you just built

Here's the part nobody does — and the part that separates a forged tool from a forged signature.

Invoke the skill on the feature you literally just shipped. Drop it into personal scope so it's there every session without ceremony — ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, auto-discovered, no team rollout, no PR, no meeting. Just you and the work. Run the skill against the real change on your screen and watch what it does: where it nails a convention, where it whiffs, where it tells you something you'd forgotten you knew. That's the daily abuse on the maker's bench — the only test that counts. And the verdict is binary in a useful way: a skill that only ever produces "use the test pyramid" tells you the forge stayed cold — you answered from memory, not the repo. A skill that surfaces something codebase-specific — the integration boundary you actually cross, the review reflex this repo enforces — tells you the conversation reached the steel.

And notice what shipping-to-yourself-first actually is: not timidity, not "I'll do the safe small version." It's the cheapest proving ground in the building. When you eventually decide to bring this skill to the team — a different conversation, on a different day — you don't arrive with a draft and a hope. You arrive with a blade you've been cutting with for a week and the nicks to prove it. The diagram below draws that crossing as what it is: deliberately downstream, dashed, and far easier because you carry evidence.

The crossing · personal bench → shared kit

Name the team-worthiness. Don't force the crossing here.

Before any promotion, ask one question: is this codebase-specific — an auth pattern, an ADR convention, a named verifier — and therefore team-worthy? Or is it a personal working-style preference that should stay yours? Naming that difference precisely is the move; the team-worthy flag drifts to mush the instant you reach for a universal like "every team should know this." Name a codebase-specific call instead. The actual crossing is a later human conversation, not an automatic PR the moment the skill compiles — and it's far easier to have when you arrive carrying a blade that has already caught something real.

Process diagram · 03The kit grows by accretion, not one big rollout. Every blade carried personal-first is a candidate the shared rack grows by — and each one leaves harder steel for the next forging.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The test isn't "looks sharp." It's "I've already cut with it."

You know the blade is real the same way the knifemaker knows: not because it looks sharp, but because you've already cut with it. Concretely: you ran the skill on the feature you just built — not on a hypothetical — and it raised something codebase-specific, not generic test-pyramid wisdom. You can say in one sentence whether it's team-worthy or personal, and why, naming a real call — an auth pattern, an ADR convention, a verifier — rather than a universal claim. The next session cold-reads it without being told, because it lives at user scope and is auto-discovered. And the negative test is the sharpest of the lot: if the SKILL.md was hand-typed in an editor and never invoked, the move didn't happen — you wrote documentation, not an instrument. This is the same discipline Agentic Engineering 101 trains the hour you author a test-strategy skill and run it on the very feature a staff engineer and a CISO are about to review.

Use when

You just did work where your judgment carried something the agent didn't have — a testing convention, a review reflex, a codebase-specific call — and you can feel it'll recur next sprint, on the next feature, for the next teammate.

Build

One forged skill at ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md — user-level, auto-discovered, weakest section already struck, cut with once on real work. Ships carried, not catalogued.

Test

It nicked something codebase-specific.
Not merely "use the test pyramid."

Core moves
Reusable on any recurring judgment — not a documentation chore.
1

Forge by conversation

Don't type it. Answer one question at a time from the repo.

2

Strike the weakest part

Make it name where the edge rolls. Push back. Don't hand over draft one.

3

Cut on real work

Carry it onto the feature you just built. Anything less is theatre.

4

Ship to your own bench

Install to ~/.claude/skills/. No review. No approval.

5

Name the team-worthiness

Codebase-specific → team-worthy. The crossing is later.

forge by conversation→ship personal→cut on real work→nicks accrue→name team-worthiness ⤳

Then it's a habit, not a chore: one skill shipped beats three drafted. Each carried blade is a candidate the shared rack grows by — and leaves harder steel for the next forging.

Why
The principle

Your codebase teaches the skill, not the manual.

"Your codebase teaches the skill, not the manual."

A skill authored on your codebase is worth more than a perfect generic one, because the value was never in the words — it was in the conventions only your repo carries. The frontier's curated skills do the work you don't re-derive: invoke, don't re-derive. But the test discipline that catches this repo's mistakes can't be downloaded. It has to be elicited, one question at a time, from the person who knows how the code actually behaves. That's why authoring is a conversation, not a markdown file: typing produces a document; conversation produces an instrument.

And personal-first isn't timidity — it's the cheapest possible proving ground. You install to your own bench, cut it on the feature in front of you, strike its weakest part, and only then does the team conversation become an option, now backed by a thing that has already caught something real. A carried-and-cut blade is evidence; a draft is only intent — evidence beats eloquence.

One skill shipped beats three drafted for an audience.
No permission required

Every part of this move happens at personal scope. The blade hangs on your own ~/.claude/skills/ and the agent auto-discovers it by name — no admin, no rollout to wait on. The forging is a normal session conversation; the cut runs on a feature you already have. The only step that touches anyone else is the shared-kit promotion — and that's deliberately downstream, a later human conversation that's easier precisely because you arrive with a blade already proving itself.

Tonight

After your next coding session — while the work is still warm.

Ten minutes. The blade lives on your personal bench by dinner; no one had to approve a thing.

  1. Pick the one judgment the agent needed from you this session — the thing only you knew because only you know this repo.
  2. Ask the agent to author a skill for it by conversation — one question at a time. Answer every question from the actual files, not from memory. "ask me one at a time about how we test here, then write the SKILL.md to ~/.claude/skills/."
  3. Make it name its own weakest section, then push back on the critique until it either holds or breaks.
  4. Drop it in ~/.claude/skills/ and invoke it on the feature you just built. Watch where the edge rolls.

You'll know it's real the same way the knifemaker knows: not because it looks sharp, but because you've already cut with it.

Where this sits

Personal → team → company. At personal scope this turns a one-off judgment into a reusable, auto-discovered instrument. At company scope it's the entry point to kit accretion: every blade carried personal-first is a candidate the shared rack grows by, so a company's compounding capability rests on how reliably its personal benches feed the shared kit. This card is the explicit prerequisite for the crossing it makes possible — team-kit promotion.

Absorption
Recipe · software lane · Absorption phase · the dispatcher after the loop closes

Sort each lesson to the clock where it fires

The principle: the loop closes when the lesson ships — but only to the clock where it'll act.

After a run you hold a fistful of lessons, and the mistake is to treat them as one bin — call the bin a skill and pour everything in. Each lesson has a clock: one acts before the run, one during it, one on the next run of this shape. Route a lesson to the wrong clock and it goes mute at exactly the moment you needed it. A private fifteen-minute pass — but also the dispatcher a company-scale context layer either institutionalises or drowns under: prevention in memory, detection in CI, reuse in skills, instead of one undifferentiated pile.

Three windows, three clocks. A skill is a repeat prescription — useless for the acute mistake you should have prevented upstream.
The dispensary image · why one counter is the wrong shape

A dispensary is three windows, not one counter.

Walk into a hospital dispensary and you do not meet a single till that does everything. You meet three windows, and each one runs on a different clock. Window one is pre-packed: the pharmacist loads the blister pack before the patient ever arrives — the drug acts before the symptom shows, the decision already made upstream, nothing to decide in the moment. Window two is stat: the dispense happens while the patient is in front of you — a check, a dose, an intervention that would be useless either earlier or later, because it only works live. Window three is the repeat prescription: the pharmacist writes it out for the next presentation of this condition — not this patient, not right now — a template that travels.

Hold that picture, because it is the whole card. After a run you are standing at the counter with a fistful of lessons, and the reflex is to shove all of them through one window labelled skill. But a lesson poured into the wrong window either spoils on the shelf or arrives after the damage is done. The three windows here — a rule in memory, a sharper check, a new skill — are the source curriculum's three-way sort, drawn from a convergent practitioner pattern read off the encode end of Armin Ronacher's reference / plan.md / verifier trio. One honest caveat that travels with every recurrence below: it's that source's sort, a useful and well-worn one — not an official Claude Code taxonomy and not a measured law. Stay open to a fourth window. What is observed is plainer than any taxonomy: a lesson filed where its clock never strikes is a lesson that goes mute.

Process diagram · 01One lesson, three windows. The question you ask decides which clock strikes — exactly one fires; the other two file it where its clock never comes round.
Use when · the moment you reach for the bundle

You're holding a short stack, and the reflex is to call it a skill.

You have just compared two runs of the same task — once un-packaged, once packaged — or post-mortemed a single bad one, and you are holding a short stack of realisations: something the agent should never have done; something that should have set off an alarm halfway through; something you want available next time this shape of task appears. The reflex is to bundle all three into a skill and call it a ship. That reflex is wrong — not because skills are bad, but because a skill only catches the next presentation. It does nothing to prevent the same mistake in this type of run, and it cannot interrupt a run already in progress. Bundling is comfortable; routing is the actual work.

This recurs at every loop closure: after any two-run compare, after a CI red that surfaces a mistake the loop should have caught, at the end of any session that produced a surprise you want the next session to inherit. The source names the trap outright — call it gap-home confusion, the practitioner observation that engineers pack everything into the second skill because skills feel like the answer. (It's a teaching note about why loops stall, not a measured rate.) Most engineers either skip the routing — everything stays in their head — or collapse it, where everything becomes a skill. Both leave the lesson mute.

The three windows · what each one is, and what it cannot do

Each window holds one kind of lesson — and refuses the others.

PREVENT — acts before the run. A rule the model reads on every invocation. Its home is a personal rules file: ./CLAUDE.local.md (gitignored, per-project) or a global equivalent. Rules are blister-packed: loaded before the session opens, invisible during it, doing their work in the negative space of things that simply do not happen. If you diagnosed a gap and a single sentence in a rules file would have closed it upstream — a habit the agent should have had from cold start — that is where it lives. Not in a skill that only fires when someone invokes it. The shape of the lesson is "the agent should never have done X."

DETECT — acts during the run. A check that fires mid-execution. Not a reminder to the agent — an actual gate: a verifier, a lint, a structural assertion, a self-critique step the agent runs before proceeding. Window two, stat. It is useless pre-packed (what would it check before anything has happened?) and useless after the fact (the damage is done). Rules prevent; they do not catch. If the diagnosis is "we never knew it had gone wrong until the very end," the lesson belongs here, in a sharpened or newly-fitted verifier — not a rule and not a skill.

REUSE — acts on the next run of this shape. A skill: a procedural template the agent invokes when it recognises this category of task again. Window three, the repeat prescription. It travels — that is its virtue. But it only fires when invoked, so it cannot prevent and it cannot interrupt. If the lesson is "I keep re-explaining this sequence from scratch," that is a skill — its home is the repeat-prescription window, and the routing stops there (how to forge it well is the next card's job, not this one's). Do not conflate a rule with a skill because the word "skill" feels satisfying to ship.

A rule that prevents a mistake upstream does more, cheaper work than a skill that re-catches it every run.

Subtraction is part of the sort · expiry is real

The same pass that stocks a packet should pull an expired one.

Routing is not only addition. The two-run contrast often shows a rule in ./CLAUDE.local.md that didn't fire, didn't help, or no longer matches how you work. The same diagnostic pass that adds a rule should ask: is there a rule already here that this new one supersedes? Cut it, visibly. A rules file that only ever grows has stopped being read honestly — it is a filing cabinet nobody opens, and a cabinet full of outdated prescriptions is not a safety net, it is noise that trains the reader, human or model, to skim. A gap can be negative: the absence the loop wants is a rule removed, not added. The source calls this compound-by-subtraction, and names the opposite as a failure mode — addition-only compounding, where you only ever add rules and never cut one.

This is the part most practitioners skip. They add the new rule, feel the satisfaction, and leave the superseded one in place "just in case." Just-in-case rules are the expired blister packs stacked at the back of the shelf. Expiry is real in a dispensary; it should be real in your rules file. The git history is your audit trail — make the deletion visible there, not just locally. The diagram below walks the same diagonal: a comfortable collapse that fires nothing, tagged legible, then filed — the cut included.

Process diagram · 02The comfortable bundle fires nothing. Sorting is what turns a stack of lessons into a loop — file each at its window, the pulled packet included.
The routing decision · ask this of each lesson

Three questions. Whichever answers first names the window.

Don't reach for the fix on the first lesson. Lay the stack out flat — three, maybe four, dominant first — so you can route them as a set, not one impulsive skill at a time. The source caps this deliberately: two runs, maybe three gaps each; pick the three that cost the most. Over-routing is its own failure; a long catalogue produces noise, not a loop. Then ask each lesson, in order:

1 · Would a rule have prevented this upstream, before the run opened? → ./CLAUDE.local.md or equivalent. Write the rule in the imperative; keep it short enough to be read, not skimmed. 2 · Would a check have caught this mid-run, while the agent still had room to correct? → tighten the verifier, add the assertion, sharpen the self-critique step. The check lives in the agent's task protocol, not in a background file. 3 · Is this a move I will need to re-perform next time this shape appears, explained from scratch every time without it? → that is a skill. One of three destinations; not the default.

If a lesson fits none cleanly, it probably wants to be a note — a post-mortem line, not a standing instruction. Notes are not windows; they are the pharmacist's handwriting on the back of the packet — useful once, not refiled as standing orders. And remember the caveat that travels with this whole sort: this taxonomy is a practitioner sort, not an official architecture. There may be a fourth window you discover. The point is not the categories; it is the habit of asking when does this need to fire? before you write anything down.

Use when

You've compared two runs of the same task — or post-mortemed one bad one — and hold a short stack of lessons, and the reflex is to bundle all of them into a skill and call it a ship. Recurs at every loop closure: after a two-run compare, after a CI red the loop should've caught.

Build

Three short artefacts at three windows — a rules file with one addition and one visible deletion; a tighter verifier or a new assertion in the task protocol; possibly a skill entry for a recurring move. The durable output is the sort itself.

Test

One named window per lesson, one sentence of why.
At least one rule pulled in git history.
Not everything a skill.

Core moves
A flat stack becomes three lessons, each at the window where its clock strikes.
1

Lay the stack out flat

Don't fix the first one. Three or four, dominant first — sort as a set.

2

Would a rule have prevented it?

A habit it should've had cold. → pre-packed (memory).

3

Would a check have caught it?

Something that fires live. → stat (sharper verifier).

4

Will I re-perform this move?

A reusable move, not the rule. → repeat rx (skill).

5

Pull the expired packet

Delete the stale rule in place. Subtraction is routing.

pre-packed (before)→stat (during)→repeat rx (next)→pull what's expired

Three clocks a lesson can strike. Send it to the wrong clock and it never strikes at all — which is why the satisfying skill bundle is the wrong default.

Monday move: pick the last run that surprised you. Write the one lesson from it as a sentence. Before you file it anywhere, ask: when would this sentence have needed to fire to change the outcome? If "before the run opened," open ./CLAUDE.local.md right now and write the rule. While you're there, read the last three rules and delete the stale one. Do that tonight; the habit compounds from the first repetition. ./CLAUDE.local.md gitignored · verifier is your own repo · skill ships to ~/.claude/skills/ · ~15 min.

What you end up with · and how you know it worked

After one diagnostic pass: a rules file with one addition and one visible deletion; a tighter verifier or a new assertion in the task protocol; possibly a skill entry for a recurring move. Three short artefacts routed to three different clocks. Each one will strike where it is needed; none will be mute.

Run the same task shape a week later and read the windows. The rule-shaped lesson does not require mention — the agent simply does not make the upstream mistake. The check-shaped lesson fires mid-run and you see it catch something. The skill-shaped lesson surfaces when the agent recognises the pattern and reaches for the template. And the structural tells: each lesson has exactly one named window, and you can say in one sentence why that window and not the other two. At least one lesson routed to memory as a deletion, the git history showing a rule pulled — pure accretion means you skipped subtraction. And not everything became a skill.

The negative test catches the most common slip: if the skill you authored reads like a documentation page describing the gap rather than moving to catch it — its description ending with a topic, not an outcome — it's mis-routed; that lesson was probably a rule. (Skill-as-documentation is the source's named diagnostic, a practitioner teaching observation about why loops stall — not a measured rate.) If you ever find yourself re-explaining something you thought you had sorted, a lesson is in the wrong window. Re-sort.

Why
The principle

The loop closes when the lesson ships — but only to the clock where it'll act.

"A skill is a repeat prescription — brilliant for chronic conditions, useless for the acute mistake you should have prevented upstream."

The consulting instinct — and the AI-tooling instinct — is to make everything a skill, because skills are the exciting artefact. They have names, they feel shipped, they feel like capability. But a skill is a repeat prescription, and a repeat prescription for an acute, preventable condition is not medicine — it is a protocol that arrives after the damage. That is precisely why undisciplined engineers route everything to the heaviest window.

The real question is temporal: at what moment in the causal chain does this lesson need to act? Rules act early and cheaply, before anything has gone wrong. Checks act at the decision point, when correction is still possible. Skills act on recurrence, when the shape repeats. Route each to the moment it is actually useful and your personal operating system starts to behave like infrastructure — silent, load-bearing, trustworthy — rather than a pile of good intentions. The compounding is asymmetric: a rule that prevents a mistake compounds silently (you never pay the tax), while a skill that arrives a lesson too late costs every time the shape recurs. Triage is not a metaphor for tidiness; it is a leverage decision. (The three windows are the source's three-way sort — a convergent practitioner pattern, not an official Claude Code taxonomy — and stay open to a fourth.)

Skills feel like the answer · which is exactly why the loop stalls.
Outcome → ⟲
Outcome → ⟲
Recipe · the wall-crossing pattern · personal → team / company

Promoting a skill to the team

The contrarian bet: the kit crosses bottom-up, never on a launch — it accretes one proven file at a time, and the announcement you were about to write is the part that fails.

A skill in your personal kit is already catching real things on real code. The move is not to roll it out — it is to let it cross the wall the same way it earned its keep: through one conversation, carried by the evidence already in your scrollback.

Everyone reaches for the launch. The launch is the part that fails.

There is a skill in your ~/.claude/skills/ directory — probably more than one — that has already caught a real thing, on real code, in your actual codebase. It encodes a convention your team argued over in two retros and then failed to apply the next sprint. You know it works because you have watched it work. Your teammate does not have it, and has no particular reason to know it exists. That gap is the wall — not political, not a process problem, just the ordinary distance between a working personal file and the shared surface where it could fire on every PR.

So you reach for the launch: a standup mention, a wiki page under "Useful tools," the ambitious version with a training session. Each of these asks people to adopt a system they did not build and have not tested on anything they own. The evidence is not theirs yet — and a busy engineer's prior for "this new process will save me time" is, deservedly, low. The wiki page goes stale. The same gap resurfaces next sprint. The announcement felt like the crossing; it was noise.

The contrarian read: a kit does not get rolled out. It accretes — and the unit of accretion is one file that already proved itself, carried by one conversation.

Before you ship anything

Name what it is

Is this skill a codebase-specific convention — your auth pattern, your ADR rule, your named integration verifier — or a personal working-style preference, like your taste on test verbosity? Promote the first; keep the second to yourself. Over-eager promotion fills the team kit with one person's opinions; over-timid leaves real codebase knowledge locked in a file everyone else re-discovers the hard way.

The principle, not a staging area

Personal first, always

It lands in ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md regardless. You run it on your own code, watch what it catches, and let the evidence accumulate in your sessions. This is the whole reason the crossing is cheap later: by the time you talk to a teammate, you are reporting a finding, not pitching an idea. The proof is already in the scrollback.

The step everyone treats as optional

Carry the evidence into one conversation

Not a roll-out — one teammate. You bring three things: what the skill caught, the convention it encodes, and where it lives. Then you open a normal code PR adding SKILL.md to .claude/skills/ in the repo, reviewed like any other diff. No sign-off, no policy doc. The evidence is the persuasion — most promotions stall here precisely because the author skipped this step, assuming the file would spread on its own.

Where a skill becomes a guarantee

Wire it into CI

A skill fires on someone's judgment; a rule fires on every PR. Once it has proven itself across a few sessions — ideally sharpened by a second author — a pre-commit hook or CI step invoking the check converts a personal win into a team guarantee. The convention argued over in two retros now fires silently before every merge, for every contributor, including the one who joined last month and never heard the argument. This is the one step that needs permission; arrive with a catch-rate number and the conversation is short.

Why bottom-up wins

A skill proven on one feature arrives with more authority than a policy doc written from first principles — the evidence is the persuasion.

The launch loses not because people are irrational but because they are busy, and a system they did not build has no claim on their attention. Accretion wins because each addition arrives with a wound it already healed. Done right, the kit's commit history reads like an archaeology of your actual production mistakes — and it carries more than one author's name. The loop runs in reverse too: every red CI build on agent-drafted code is diagnostic — if it caught a real mistake, ask what rule in CLAUDE.local.md would have caught it upstream, and if none exists, write it. Rules grow from real failures, never prophylactic policy.

There is a wall behind the wall.

The failure mode hides well because it looks like success: you mention the skill, a couple of people say "oh nice," it gets added to the wiki — and it never fires in anyone else's session. So make the test falsifiable. The pattern crossed when a teammate invokes the skill unprompted, in their own session, on a PR you did not write. If you have to mention it at standup for it to get used, only the announcement crossed. Better still: a teammate proposes a sharpening from their own invocation evidence — now they are in the encode loop, not just consuming it. Clearing that second wall is the whole point.

What to do Monday

Open ~/.claude/skills/ and find one skill you invoked at least twice this week. Decide: codebase-specific, or personal preference? If it is codebase-specific, draft a two-sentence opener — what it catches, and where it lives in the kit — and send it to one teammate before end of day. That is the entire move. Everything up to and through the conversation needs nothing but the evidence you already have; only the mandatory CI gate needs anyone's permission, and that ask is easy once a teammate has used the skill by choice.

The wall does not come down with a launch. It comes down one proven file at a time — and the next agent that cold-starts on the repo reads a kit that already knows what yours learned the hard way.

Outcome → ⟲
Recipe · software · Outcome → ⟲ · the Outcome-end move

Reading your own arc

A word is defined by its citations, not by how you remember using it — and the loop only closes when the lesson ships: narrated from the files, pruned to what still fires.

A lexicographer never defines a word from how they remember using it — they read the dated slips where it was caught in the wild, written by people with no stake in the meaning. After a stretch of real work, your arc is the word and your artefacts are the slips: the ./CLAUDE.local.md that grew rule by rule, the ADRs, the skills, the RUN-NOTES.md. So don't write the definition. Hand the slips to a reader who was never in the room, make it read the arc back, then cut the rules the read proves stale.

The specimen · the page itselfThe card is the deliverable. On the left, the arc you'd narrate from the chair — all wins, source line blank — struck through. On the right, the field note a fresh agent wrote from the files, every claim trailing the slip it came from. (The arc-retrospective and the bounded read are the source's read-from-your-own-evidence discipline, not a vendor feature; "a fresh agent can't flatter you" is the rationale, never a measured property. The illustrative citations are carried from the card's own exemplars.)
The reading · do this Monday

Hand the slips to a reader who was never in the room — then cut one rule the read proves stale.

  1. Open a fresh Claude Code session in the repo where your last real arc of work lives — an agent with no memory of it, so it can't keep your wins and quietly edit the dead ends. Hand it a bounded read-list, named files, not the whole history: the root rules file, ./CLAUDE.local.md, the memory folder, any ADRs, every skill in ~/.claude/skills/ you authored there, the last run's RUN-NOTES.md. Each was written in the moment with no incentive to look good later — which is exactly what makes it the honest record.
  2. Ask for one page, in the instruction that does the work: write from my artefacts, quote me where you can, skip the summary of what the training taught. Require it to quote your own files back — if it can't point to the line a claim came from, it narrated from your chair. Re-run with quote-required.
  3. Reject any line that reads like a trainer monologue — "this journey taught me to embrace…" The slips don't talk like that. If a stranger could mistake the page for marketing copy, the voice slipped; send it back to the files.
  4. Read the page against your own memory and mark where the evidence disagrees with your story. Then, while you're in the rules file, find one rule the arc just made stale — superseded, or no longer matching how you work — and delete it in place, the deletion visible in git. A file that only grows is one nobody re-reads; the arc-read is where you earn the right to shrink the kit.
  5. Ship the page where the next session reads first — an ADR, an observations/ memo, or a file you'll point an agent at. Not a diary entry: the cold-start brief for whoever inherits the repo, teammate or future-you. The loop closes when the lesson ships.

This is the hinge between "I learned this" and "the org keeps it."
